subject: physics
summary: Ohm's law, resistor networks, Kirchhoff, Wheatstone bridge, potentiometer, meter bridge, drift velocity, internal resistance, and EMF/terminal-voltage distinctions.

formulas.name: Resistance from resistivity
formulas.note: Stretching a wire uniformly: $R \propto L^2$ (since $V$ constant).

formulas.name: Kirchhoff's laws
formulas.expr: $\sum I = 0$ at junction; $\sum V = 0$ around loop

formulas.name: Wheatstone balance
formulas.note: No current through galvanometer at balance.

formulas.name: Meter bridge
formulas.note: $l$ in cm, balancing length from $R$ side.

shortcuts: Balanced Wheatstone: P/Q = R/S — the galvanometer arm collapses; ignore the middle resistor in any further network calc.
Equal resistors in parallel: R_each/N. For N=2 equal: product/sum shortcut R/2.
Cells in series: EMF adds, r adds. Cells in parallel (identical): EMF same, r/N.
For maximum power transfer, external R = internal r; then P_max = \varepsilon^2/(4r).
Potentiometer is a NULL method — no current drawn, so it measures true EMF (not terminal V).
If wire stretched to n times length (volume constant): new R = n^2 × R_old.
Meter bridge unknowns go on the LEFT gap by convention; if balancing length > 50 cm, unknown < known.
For a cube of 12 equal R's across body diagonal: R_eq = 5R/6; across face diagonal: 3R/4; across edge: 7R/12.
traps: V_terminal = EMF − I·r (minus, while discharging). Students often write plus.
Ammeter has LOW resistance (in series); voltmeter has HIGH resistance (in parallel). Swapping them burns the meter.
Drift velocity is of the order of mm/s, but signal travels at ~c because the field propagates, not the electrons.
In potentiometer, increasing driver cell EMF shifts balance length — it doesn't mean the measured EMF changed.
Resistivity ρ is material property; resistance R depends on geometry. Don't conflate.
Power rating on a bulb is at rated voltage; actual P = V_applied^2 / R_bulb, NOT the label value if voltage differs.
Kirchhoff's voltage law: be consistent with sign when traversing EMF (− to + is +ε; + to − is −ε).
examDayCheck: Read all circuit diagrams left-to-right; mark current directions before writing KVL.
If a Wheatstone is balanced, delete the galvanometer branch immediately.
For cells questions: check if it's discharge (V = ε − Ir) or charging (V = ε + Ir).
When asked for 'heat produced in time t', use H = I^2Rt (Joule), not just P.
Units: resistivity Ω·m, conductivity S/m, current density A/m^2.

subject: physics
summary: Coulomb's law, electric field/potential, Gauss's law, capacitors, dielectrics, energy storage, and potential energy of dipole/charge configurations.

formulas.name: Field of infinite sheet / line / shell

shortcuts: Inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium: E = 0; surface is equipotential; charge resides on outer surface.
Connected in SERIES, capacitors store the SAME charge; in PARALLEL, the SAME voltage.
Battery CONNECTED + dielectric inserted: V fixed, C↑, Q↑, U↑. Battery DISCONNECTED + dielectric: Q fixed, C↑, V↓, U↓.
Dipole in uniform E: net force = 0, only torque. In non-uniform E: also net force toward stronger field.
Shell theorem: treat a uniformly charged spherical shell as a point charge at its centre — but ONLY for points OUTSIDE.
If two charged drops merge (volume conservative): new radius R' = n^(1/3)·R; V' = n^(2/3)·V.
Equipotential surfaces are always ⟂ to E-field lines. Work done moving a charge along an equipotential = 0.
traps: Flux through a closed surface depends ONLY on enclosed charge — external charges contribute 0 net flux (they create field but zero net flux).
Electric field is a vector; potential is scalar. Two points can have same V but different E (and vice versa).
W = q(V_A − V_B) moves charge from A to B; sign matters. Positive external work is needed to move +q against E.
Capacitance depends only on geometry + dielectric, NEVER on charge or voltage applied.
Dielectric strength ≠ dielectric constant. Strength is breakdown field (V/m); constant K is dimensionless.
Electrostatic PE of a system = sum over PAIRS, not over charges — for 3 charges, you have 3 pairs.
At the centre of a uniformly charged ring, E = 0 but V ≠ 0 (V = kQ/R).
examDayCheck: Sketch field lines before computing — they reveal symmetry for Gauss's law.
For capacitor changes: first decide 'battery connected?' → that fixes V or Q.
Units: flux in N·m²/C or V·m; capacitance in Farad = C/V.
K (dielectric constant) always ≥ 1; it multiplies C and divides E/V inside.
For dipole, memorise factor 2 for axial and identify 'ideal' (point) dipole vs physical.

subject: physics
summary: Newton's laws, friction, pulleys, pseudo-forces in non-inertial frames, circular motion, and free-body diagrams for coupled systems.
shortcuts: In a connected-block problem, treat the whole system to get a, then isolate one block for T.
If μ·cotθ ≥ 1, block will NOT slide on its own down an incline (static friction holds).
For a body on a rough incline pushed UP: a = −g(sinθ + μcosθ). Deceleration is larger than smooth case.
In a lift accelerating UP at a: apparent weight = m(g+a); DOWN: m(g−a); free-fall: 0.
Minimum speed at top of vertical loop: v_top = √(gR). At bottom then: v_bot = √(5gR).
Rope/string assumed massless & inextensible unless told otherwise → tension same throughout, accelerations linked.
Friction is self-adjusting up to f_s,max — don't set f = μN when object is static and another force is smaller.
traps: Static friction acts OPPOSITE to intended (or impending) motion, not actual motion.
On a rough horizontal surface, minimum force to MOVE a block = μ_s mg, but once moving, only μ_k mg maintains motion.
Normal force ≠ mg when surface is inclined or vertical acceleration is non-zero (e.g., lift, inclined plane, banked road).
Centripetal 'force' is a requirement, not a new force — it's provided by tension/friction/gravity/normal.
Banking angle design is for ONE speed only (optimum). Above/below needs friction.
In Atwood problems, T is SAME magnitude on both sides for an ideal pulley but its direction differs per block.
Newton's 3rd-law pair acts on DIFFERENT bodies — never cancel them in a single FBD.
examDayCheck: Draw the FBD for EACH body separately. Label only forces ACTING ON that body.
Pick a sensible axis (along incline, for instance) to minimise component algebra.
Check: does a come out negative? If so, either direction assumption was wrong, or motion doesn't start.
g = 10 m/s² unless stated; mass in kg, F in N. Always verify units.
For circular motion, identify what PROVIDES the centripetal force before writing equations.

subject: physics
summary: Work-energy theorem, conservative forces, potential energy, elastic vs inelastic collisions, power, and spring energy.
shortcuts: Elastic collision, equal masses, second at rest: they swap velocities (v1'=0, v2'=u1).
Elastic collision, heavy hits light at rest: light flies off at ≈ 2u; heavy barely slows.
Elastic, light hits heavy at rest: light rebounds with ~ −u; heavy barely moves.
Conservative force ⇔ closed-loop work = 0 ⇔ F = −dU/dx. Gravity, spring, electrostatic: conservative. Friction, viscous: NOT.
For variable F(x): W = ∫F dx (area under F-x curve). For F(t): use impulse for Δp, then work–energy.
Fractional KE transfer in elastic collision (target at rest): 4m1m2/(m1+m2)^2 — max when m1 = m2 (100% transfer).
If asked 'minimum v at bottom so particle completes vertical circle': answer √(5gR); if 'just crosses horizontal diameter': √(3gR).
traps: Work done by a centripetal force = 0 (force ⟂ displacement). Same for normal force on a sliding body, tension in a circular swing.
KE cannot be negative. PE can be (just depends on reference).
Momentum is conserved in EVERY collision (if external F = 0). KE conserved ONLY in elastic collisions.
Spring PE = ½kx² regardless of direction of stretch (x could be negative but x² is positive).
Power 'P' in a machine lifting mass m at constant v up against gravity: P = mgv — not mav (a=0).
Friction always does negative work on the moving body; but it can do POSITIVE work on the body it drags along (e.g., conveyor belt).
'Average power' ≠ F·v_avg in general; use W_total / t_total.
examDayCheck: Decide: is the force conservative? If yes, use energy conservation — it's faster than force + kinematics.
For collisions, list conservation laws BEFORE plugging: momentum always; KE only if elastic.
Check: is the answer in Joules (work/energy) or Watts (power)?
If PE reference isn't specified, set it where convenient (usually lowest point) — final answer is Δ, not U.
For a pulley/spring system, energy conservation is usually faster than Newton's laws.

subject: physics
summary: Moment of inertia, torque, angular momentum, rolling without slipping, parallel/perpendicular axis theorems, and rotational KE.

formulas.name: I of common bodies (about CM axis)
formulas.expr: Ring $MR^2$; Disc $\tfrac12 MR^2$; Solid sphere $\tfrac25 MR^2$; Hollow sphere $\tfrac23 MR^2$; Rod (perp, centre) $ML^2/12$

shortcuts: Rolling down an incline: Solid sphere (fastest) > Solid cylinder > Hollow sphere > Hollow cylinder (slowest). Order = (1 + I/MR²) smaller → faster.
For a body 'rolling without slipping', friction does ZERO work (point of contact is momentarily at rest).
If external torque = 0, L is conserved — skater pulling arms in: I↓ so ω↑, KE↑ (work done by muscles).
Parallel axis: d is distance from CM-axis to new parallel axis. Only applies if axes are parallel.
Perpendicular axis applies ONLY to planar (2D) laminae. Useful: for a ring about diameter, I = MR²/2.
For a uniform rod of length L about end (perpendicular): I = ML²/3 (via parallel axis from centre).
Rolling starts pure slipping; friction converts translational → rotational until v = Rω — then steady rolling.
traps: Moment of inertia depends on axis chosen — always specify axis before computing.
Torque is r × F, not F × r (direction matters). Use right-hand rule.
Angular velocity ω is same for all points on a rigid body; linear v = ωr differs with r.
A body can have zero angular momentum about one axis but non-zero about another (choose axis wisely).
Centre of mass of a uniform body isn't always at geometric centre when mass distribution is non-uniform.
KE of rolling body is NOT just ½mv² — add ½Iω². Total = ½mv²(1 + I/mR²).
In pure rolling, point of contact's velocity = 0 (not just small), and top point's velocity = 2v_cm.
examDayCheck: For ring/disc/sphere I questions: recite 'ring MR², disc MR²/2, solid sphere 2MR²/5, hollow 2MR²/3'.
Check axis: if not through CM, use parallel axis (add Md²).
For rolling questions, always check 'without slipping' condition before applying v = Rω.
If torque about a point is 0, L about THAT point is conserved — even if other forces act.
Units: I in kg·m²; τ in N·m; L in kg·m²/s or J·s.

subject: physics
summary: Newton's law of gravitation, g variation with altitude/depth/latitude, orbital mechanics, escape velocity, Kepler's laws, and gravitational PE.
shortcuts: v_e = √2 × v_o — escape speed is √2 times orbital speed at same radius.
Geostationary orbit: T = 24 h, r ≈ 42 000 km from Earth's centre (~36 000 km altitude), equatorial, west-to-east.
Energy to move satellite from orbit r₁ to r₂: ΔE = (GMm/2)(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
At height h = R (one Earth-radius up), g reduces to g/4.
At depth d = R/2, g drops to g/2. At centre (d = R): g = 0.
Weight at equator < weight at pole (Earth's rotation and bulge). Δg ≈ Rω²cos²λ.
For a binary-star or two-body orbit, use reduced mass μ = m₁m₂/(m₁+m₂) and total separation.
traps: U_gravitational is NEGATIVE for bound systems. U = 0 at infinity by convention.
Escape velocity is INDEPENDENT of angle of projection (as long as no air) and of projectile mass.
Kepler's 3rd law: T² ∝ a³ where a is SEMI-MAJOR axis (not radius for elliptic orbit).
At orbital height, satellite is NOT weightless — it's in free-fall toward Earth; gravity provides centripetal force.
Shell theorem: inside a uniform spherical shell, gravitational field = 0 (but potential is constant, non-zero).
Don't mix g (acceleration, m/s²) with G (universal constant, N·m²/kg²).
Orbital speed DECREASES with radius (v ∝ 1/√r) — higher orbit means slower but longer period.
examDayCheck: Check: is the question using R (Earth radius) or r (orbit radius)? They differ when satellite is at height h.
For energy questions, remember total E < 0 for bound, = 0 at escape, > 0 for unbound.
g at pole > g at equator; g decreases both with altitude and depth (at different rates).
Kepler: same orbit → equal areas in equal times. Planet moves fastest at perihelion, slowest at aphelion.
Units: G in N·m²/kg²; g in m/s²; v_e in km/s (Earth's is 11.2).

subject: physics
summary: Biot-Savart, Ampere's law, force on current-carrying wires and charged particles, solenoid/toroid fields, moving-coil galvanometer, and magnetic materials.
shortcuts: Right-hand rule: thumb = I, fingers curl = B direction for a wire. For a loop, fingers = I, thumb = north pole (m direction).
Parallel currents ATTRACT; antiparallel REPEL (mnemonic: 'like-minded friends hug').
Inside a long solenoid, B is uniform and axial; outside, B ≈ 0.
A charged particle entering B with v ⟂ B: circular motion (constant speed). v ∥ B: straight line. General: helix.
Velocity selector: qE = qvB → v = E/B. Only this speed passes through undeviated.
Cyclotron frequency: f = qB/(2πm) — independent of radius or energy (for non-relativistic).
For a bar magnet, neutral points lie on the equatorial line (in Earth's field) at distance where B_magnet = B_Horizontal.
Period of oscillation of a magnet in Earth's field: T = 2π√(I/MB_H).
traps: Magnetic force does NO work on a charged particle (F ⟂ v always). Speed constant; only direction changes.
Solenoid formula B = μ₀nI requires 'long' solenoid and points INSIDE (not at ends — there B is halved).
Biot-Savart's dB at a point on a wire's own extension = 0 (sin 0° = 0).
An ammeter has LOW resistance (shunt in parallel); a voltmeter has HIGH resistance (series with coil). Don't swap.
Magnetic moment m of a loop = N·I·A (include number of turns N).
Earth's magnetic north pole is a magnetic SOUTH (since it attracts a compass's north). Dip angle δ, not inclination.
Diamagnetic substances have χ < 0 (slightly); paramagnetic χ > 0 (small); ferromagnetic χ ≫ 1.
examDayCheck: Identify geometry: straight wire, loop, solenoid, toroid — each has a specific B formula.
For charged particles in B: write qvB = mv²/r to get r; T = 2πm/(qB) is velocity-independent.
Check direction with right-hand rule; ×/⊙ for into/out of page.
Shunt formula: S < G (shunt is small); voltmeter series R ≫ G.
Units: B in Tesla (T), m in A·m², μ₀ = 4π×10⁻⁷ T·m/A.

subject: physics
summary: Faraday's/Lenz's laws, motional EMF, self and mutual inductance, LR/LC/LCR circuits, AC power, resonance, and transformers.
shortcuts: Lenz's law = energy conservation: induced current OPPOSES the change in flux. Memorise direction, don't re-derive.
At resonance in LCR: X_L = X_C, Z = R (minimum), I = maximum, power factor = 1.
Purely inductive or purely capacitive circuit: avg power = 0 (phase ±90°).
Transformer: step-up (N_s > N_p) → V up, I down. Step-down: opposite.
RMS = Peak/√2 for sinusoidal AC. For full-wave rectified: same. For half-wave: I_0/2 (mean), I_0/2 (rms).
Skin effect: at HF, current flows on surface — use stranded wires.
Eddy currents: minimised by laminating the iron core (transformer/motor), so currents can't loop freely.
traps: Sign: Faraday ε = −dΦ/dt. The minus encodes Lenz — don't drop it.
Induced current direction OPPOSES change in flux, not flux itself — flux decreasing → induced current sustains it.
In a DC circuit at STEADY STATE: inductor = wire (X_L = 0); capacitor = open (X_C = ∞).
Motional EMF BLv requires B ⟂ v ⟂ L (all mutually perpendicular). Otherwise use components.
Peak-to-peak ≠ peak ≠ rms. For V_0 = 100 V peak: peak-to-peak = 200 V, rms ≈ 70.7 V.
In LCR, at resonance I max but it doesn't mean V max across each element — V_L = V_C individually can be many times V_source.
Transformer doesn't work on DC — only changing flux induces EMF in secondary.
examDayCheck: If asked about 'induced EMF', always check flux change first, then direction via Lenz.
In AC questions: identify L, C, R, frequency → compute X_L, X_C → Z, I, phase.
For transformer: energy conservation means V_p·I_p = V_s·I_s (ideal).
Resonance peaks — off-resonance, current drops sharply (sharpness = Q-factor).
Units: L in Henry (H), Φ in Weber (Wb = V·s), EMF in Volt.

subject: physics
summary: Reflection, refraction, lens/mirror formula, total internal reflection, prism dispersion, and optical instruments.

formulas.name: Prism deviation
formulas.expr: $\delta = i_1 + i_2 - A$; at min: $\delta_m = 2i - A$, $n = \sin\tfrac{A+\delta_m}{2}/\sin\tfrac{A}{2}$

shortcuts: Sign convention: distances measured from optical centre/pole, along incident light direction = positive; opposite = negative. Heights above axis = positive.
Converging lens/mirror: f > 0. Diverging: f < 0. For mirror, concave f < 0 (new convention) BUT NCERT + KCET uses 'concave f < 0' — follow NCERT Cartesian.
If image is REAL, v is positive for lens (opposite side), negative for mirror (same side).
TIR requires denser → rarer AND i > θ_c. Used in optical fibres, prisms.
Apparent depth: d_app = d_real × (n_obs/n_medium). Pool looks shallower when viewed from air.
Combination of thin lenses in contact: powers add directly. Separated by d: 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ − d/(f₁f₂).
For a prism of small angle A: δ ≈ (n−1)A. Chromatic dispersion: δ_V > δ_R (violet bends more).
traps: Sign convention in lens formula: distances measured from optical centre in direction of light are positive. Apply consistently — mixing conventions gives wrong sign of f.
Mirror formula has +1/u and +1/v; lens formula has −1/u (NOT +). Don't conflate.
Focal length of a lens depends on surrounding medium! If n_lens = n_medium, f → ∞ (no refraction).
A concave mirror produces a VIRTUAL image when object is between pole and focus — erect and magnified.
Power of a diverging lens is NEGATIVE.
Image at least distance of distinct vision (D=25cm) gives maximum M for microscope/simple magnifier.
Prism: minimum deviation ≠ 0 deviation. At min deviation, i = e, ray inside is parallel to base.
examDayCheck: Draw a quick ray diagram even for MCQ — reveals sign of magnification and real/virtual.
Check: is it a mirror or lens formula? Mirror uses +, lens uses − for 1/u.
For combination: add powers (not focal lengths).
For TIR: first check denser→rarer before computing θ_c.
Units: f in cm (typical); P = 1/f where f MUST be in metres → dioptre.

subject: physics
summary: Huygens' principle, interference (Young's experiment), diffraction, polarisation, and thin-film/resolving-power basics.

formulas.name: Thin film (reflected, normal)
formulas.expr: $2\mu t = (n+\tfrac12)\lambda$ (constructive, w/ phase change at top)

formulas.name: Frequency (wave)
formulas.expr: $f = c/\lambda$ (vacuum); wavelength changes in medium, frequency stays the same

shortcuts: Fringe width β ∝ λD/d. Increase D → wider fringes. Use denser medium (λ↓) → narrower.
When YDSE is immersed in water (n=4/3): β decreases by factor 4/3.
Central maximum in YDSE is BRIGHT (zero path difference). Shift of pattern due to slab of thickness t: Δy = (μ−1)tD/d.
In single-slit, central maximum is 2× wider than side maxima and carries ~84% of intensity.
Unpolarised light through a polariser → intensity halves (I_0/2). Then Malus applies for subsequent analyser.
Brewster angle: reflected light fully polarised (⟂ plane of incidence). θ_B + θ_r = 90°.
Wavelength in medium: λ_m = λ_vacuum / n. Frequency unchanged across boundary.
traps: β = λD/d — small d gives WIDE fringes. Students often think opposite.
In single-slit diffraction, minima are at a·sinθ = nλ (NOT maxima). In YDSE (double-slit) n·λ gives MAXIMA.
Intensity in YDSE: I_max = 4I_0 (if I_1 = I_2 = I_0) and I_min = 0. Ratio I_max:I_min = (√I_1+√I_2)²:(√I_1−√I_2)².
Brewster's angle depends on wavelength (via n) — not a single universal value.
Polarisation needs TRANSVERSE waves — light yes, sound no. Used to prove light is transverse.
'Coherent sources' means constant phase difference — NOT zero phase difference.
Resolving power improves with LARGER aperture (D) and SHORTER wavelength (λ).
examDayCheck: Memorise β = λD/d — the single most-tested YDSE formula.
Check: is it YDSE (n·λ = max) or single-slit (a·sinθ = n·λ for minima)?
For polariser stack: I_0 → I_0/2 after 1st (unpolarised). Then Malus for each subsequent.
When medium changes (immersed, slab), update λ_medium = λ_vacuum/n.
Units: λ in nm or Å (1 Å = 0.1 nm); D in metres; d usually in mm.

subject: physics
summary: Bohr model, hydrogen spectral series, nuclear composition, binding energy, radioactive decay, and mass-energy relation.

formulas.name: Hydrogen series
formulas.expr: Lyman (n→1, UV); Balmer (n→2, visible); Paschen (n→3, IR)

shortcuts: Bohr ground state H: E = −13.6 eV, r = 0.529 Å. For He⁺ (Z=2): E × 4, r × 1/2.
Ionisation energy of H = 13.6 eV; excitation to n=2 takes 10.2 eV (Lyman-α).
Number of spectral lines from n-th level = n(n−1)/2.
Half-life → 1/2 every t_{1/2}. After n half-lives: fraction left = (1/2)^n.
BE per nucleon peaks at ~A=56 (Fe). Fission of heavy AND fusion of light both release energy.
α-decay: A−4, Z−2. β⁻-decay: A same, Z+1. γ-decay: no change in A, Z.
De Broglie: λ = h/p. Electron accelerated through V volts: λ = 12.27/√V Å.
traps: E_n for H is NEGATIVE (bound state). n=∞ → E=0 (free electron).
Bohr model applies STRICTLY only to hydrogenic (one-electron) atoms: H, He⁺, Li²⁺.
In transition n_i → n_f, emitted photon energy = E_i − E_f. Make sure n_f < n_i for emission.
Rydberg's formula gives 1/λ, not λ directly. And the larger quantum number MUST be n_2.
Mass defect is always POSITIVE (bound nucleus is lighter than free constituents).
Half-life is CONSTANT for given nuclide — not affected by temperature, pressure, or chemical state.
Number of α + β emissions: compare initial (A₀, Z₀) to final. Δα = ΔA/4, then Δβ⁻ from Z.
examDayCheck: Quick lookup: 13.6/n² eV for H energies.
For transitions: compute E_photon = |ΔE|, then λ = hc/E (hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm).
For half-life problems: after nT half-lives, N = N₀/2ⁿ.
For BE/nucleon: higher means more stable — Fe (A=56) is peak.
Units: Å for atomic radii; eV for atomic energies; MeV for nuclear.

subject: physics
summary: First and second laws, isothermal/adiabatic/isobaric/isochoric processes, heat engines, Carnot cycle, refrigerator efficiency, and entropy basics.

formulas.name: First law
formulas.note: Sign convention: W done BY gas is positive.

shortcuts: Adiabatic: Q = 0, so ΔU = −W. In EXPANSION, gas cools; in COMPRESSION, gas heats.
Isothermal: ΔU = 0 (ideal gas), so Q = W. Slow process in contact with reservoir.
Cyclic process: ΔU = 0 over a cycle, so Q_net = W_net = area enclosed on p-V diagram.
Carnot's η depends only on temperatures (in Kelvin), not on working substance.
Monatomic gas: C_v = 3R/2, C_p = 5R/2, γ = 5/3. Diatomic: C_v = 5R/2, C_p = 7R/2, γ = 7/5.
Slope on p-V: adiabatic > isothermal. Adiabatic is steeper (factor γ).
Refrigerator: COP can be > 1 (β is NOT an efficiency). Max COP is Carnot: T_c/(T_h−T_c).
traps: In the first law Q = ΔU + W (Physics convention, W by gas) — don't confuse with chemistry convention (W on gas).
Adiabatic means Q = 0 (NOT isothermal). Often confused.
Internal energy U of ideal gas depends ONLY on T — for isothermal, ΔU = 0 even if V, p change.
Carnot η uses temperatures in KELVIN, not Celsius. η = 1 − T_c/T_h.
Free expansion into vacuum: W = 0, Q = 0 → ΔU = 0, T constant (for ideal gas).
Work done ON gas is NEGATIVE of work done BY gas. Be consistent.
No engine can have η = 100% (would violate 2nd law). A reversible engine between T_h, T_c has max η = 1 − T_c/T_h.
examDayCheck: Identify process FIRST: isothermal/adiabatic/isobaric/isochoric. That fixes which quantity is 0.
Check: Kelvin for Carnot; don't plug °C.
For p-V cycles: area enclosed = net W. Clockwise = heat engine (W > 0); counter = refrigerator.
If asked 'what's ΔU' — for ideal gas, only T matters. ΔU = nC_v ΔT.
Units: R = 8.314 J/(mol·K); Q, W, U in Joules; T in Kelvin.

subject: physics
summary: SHM kinematics, energy, pendulum/spring oscillators, superposition, beats, standing waves, Doppler effect, and wave speed on strings/in gases.

formulas.name: Energy in SHM
formulas.expr: $E = \tfrac12 m\omega^2 A^2$; KE max at x=0, PE max at x=±A

formulas.name: Doppler (general)
formulas.note: Top sign: observer toward source / source toward observer.

shortcuts: In SHM, at x = A/2: KE = 3E/4, PE = E/4.
For two springs in parallel: k_eff = k₁ + k₂; in series: 1/k_eff = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂.
A simple pendulum's T is INDEPENDENT of mass. In a lift accelerating up at a: T = 2π√(L/(g+a)).
Open pipe: all harmonics (f, 2f, 3f, ...). Closed pipe: only odd (f, 3f, 5f, ...).
String vibration modes: n loops in length L → λ = 2L/n; frequency n·(v/2L).
Beats heard when two frequencies differ by < ~10 Hz. Above that, ear hears them separately.
Doppler: frequency INCREASES when observer and source approach; DECREASES on separation. No shift if motion is perpendicular.
traps: SHM requires F = −kx (restoring, linearly proportional). Pendulum only SHM for small θ (sin θ ≈ θ).
In SHM, acceleration is MAX at extremes (x = ±A), ZERO at mean (x = 0). Velocity is opposite.
For a vertical spring with mass: new equilibrium is mg/k below natural length, but T is still 2π√(m/k).
Wave speed v on a string doesn't depend on frequency — only on tension and linear density.
Speed of sound in a gas is INDEPENDENT of pressure (at fixed T) but depends on T: v ∝ √T.
Beats: if tuning fork filed → f↑. Two forks beat at 4 Hz: unknown could be f±4, not just one.
Doppler formula sign: depends on convention — check toward/away for source AND observer separately.
examDayCheck: SHM period questions: identify k or L/g, then T = 2π√(m/k) or 2π√(L/g).
For waves on strings/pipes, count nodes/antinodes from diagram to get mode number.
Doppler: write general formula, plug signs based on 'approaching = +' rule.
Beat frequency = |difference| of two frequencies.
Units: ω in rad/s, f in Hz, T in s. k = 2π/λ is wave number, not spring constant — context matters.

subject: physics
summary: Photoelectric effect, Einstein's equation, threshold/work function, de Broglie wavelength, and matter-wave experiments.
shortcuts: Photoelectric emission happens only when ν ≥ ν₀ (frequency threshold), regardless of intensity.
Increasing intensity (same ν): MORE photoelectrons (higher current) but SAME KE_max.
Increasing frequency: SAME number of electrons per photon absorbed, but HIGHER KE_max.
Stopping potential V₀ depends ONLY on frequency and metal (work function), NOT on intensity.
De Broglie: λ = h/p. For massive, slow particles λ is vanishingly small; for electrons λ is Å scale.
At same KE, λ_electron > λ_proton (since p = √(2mKE), smaller m → smaller p → larger λ).
Photon has zero rest mass but momentum p = E/c = h/λ.
traps: Work function φ (eV) and threshold wavelength λ₀ are INVERSELY related: larger φ ↔ smaller λ₀.
Photoelectric effect is INSTANTANEOUS — no time lag, disproving the wave-only model of light.
KE_max (not 'KE'): photoelectrons have a SPECTRUM of KE from 0 to KE_max (those at surface have max).
Classical wave theory CANNOT explain threshold frequency, instant emission, or KE independent of intensity.
De Broglie works for all matter but measurable only for small m (electrons yes; cricket ball no).
Momentum of photon: p = h/λ. Don't use mv (m_rest = 0).
Convert units: 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J; hc ≈ 1240 eV·nm. Keep all quantities in same unit family.
examDayCheck: Identify 'above or below threshold?' — if ν < ν₀, no emission no matter the intensity.
For stopping potential: eV₀ = hν − φ. Graph V₀ vs ν is a straight line of slope h/e.
For de Broglie, compute p first (from KE or direct), then λ = h/p.
Quick: electron through V volts → λ = 12.27/√V Å.
Units: φ in eV (typical), λ in nm or Å, h = 6.63×10⁻³⁴ J·s = 4.14×10⁻¹⁵ eV·s.

subject: chemistry
summary: SN1/SN2/E1/E2 mechanics, reagent matching, and the special inertness of haloarenes.

formulas.name: SN2 mechanism
formulas.note: One step, backside attack, Walden inversion, 2nd-order kinetics.

formulas.name: SN1 mechanism
formulas.expr: R-X $\rightarrow$ R$^+$ + X$^-$ (slow); R$^+$ + Nu$^-$ $\rightarrow$ R-Nu
formulas.note: Two-step, racemisation, 1st-order; carbocation stability controls rate.

formulas.name: Saytzeff elimination
formulas.expr: E1/E2 give the MORE substituted (stable) alkene as major

formulas.name: Gattermann
formulas.expr: ArN$_2^+$ + Cu/HCl or HBr $\rightarrow$ Ar-Cl/Br (poorer yield than Sandmeyer)

shortcuts: SN2 rate: CH$_3$X > 1° > 2° > 3° (steric); SN1 rate is the REVERSE (cation stability).
Leaving group ability: I > Br > Cl > F (bigger, weaker C-X; F is worst LG).
Polar protic solvent (H$_2$O, ROH) favours SN1/E1; polar aprotic (DMSO, DMF, acetone) favours SN2.
Allyl/benzyl halides: undergo BOTH SN1 and SN2 readily (resonance-stabilised cation AND unhindered).
Vinyl and aryl halides: INERT to SN1/SN2 (sp$^2$ C, partial double-bond character, back-donation).
Chlorobenzene EAS: -Cl is o/p-directing but deactivating (resonance donor, inductive withdrawer).
DDT = dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane; Freon = CF$_2$Cl$_2$ (ozone killer); CHCl$_3$ stored in dark (phosgene).
traps: Anti-Markovnikov addition is HBr-only (peroxide/Kharasch effect); HCl and HI do NOT show it.
Nucleophilicity vs basicity in polar protic: I$^-$ > Br$^-$ > Cl$^-$ > F$^-$ (opposite of gas phase).
Aryl halides react with strong base (NaNH$_2$) via BENZYNE, not SN2.
Neopentyl halide (CH$_3$)$_3$CCH$_2$X is 1° but DOES NOT do SN2 (β-steric block).
CHCl$_3$ + aq. NaOH + RNH$_2$ $\rightarrow$ RNC (carbylamine) — only 1° amines.
Racemic mixture is optically INACTIVE; meso is also inactive (internal plane).
examDayCheck: Read 1°/2°/3° + solvent polarity $\rightarrow$ pick SN1 vs SN2 in one glance.
Benzyl/allyl = 'best of both worlds'; vinyl/aryl = 'does nothing'.
If base is bulky $\rightarrow$ Hofmann; if base is small $\rightarrow$ Saytzeff.
Ar-N$_2^+$ at 0–5 °C: Cl/Br/CN needs Cu (Sandmeyer); I needs just KI.

subject: chemistry
summary: Acidity ladder, Lucas test, Williamson synthesis, Reimer–Tiemann and Kolbe — all reagent-match gold.

formulas.name: Acidity order
formulas.expr: RCOOH > H$_2$CO$_3$ > ArOH > H$_2$O > ROH > HC$\equiv$CH

formulas.name: Lucas test (anhyd. ZnCl$_2$/HCl)
formulas.expr: 3° ROH: instant turbidity; 2°: 5–10 min; 1°: no reaction at RT

formulas.name: Williamson ether synth
formulas.expr: R-ONa + R$'$-X $\rightarrow$ R-O-R$'$ + NaX (SN2; must use 1° R$'$-X)

shortcuts: Phenol > alcohol in acidity: phenoxide is resonance-stabilised; alkoxide is not.
Electron-withdrawing groups (NO$_2$, especially o/p) INCREASE phenol acidity; alkyl groups decrease.
p-nitrophenol > m-nitrophenol acidity (resonance vs only inductive).
Williamson for 3°-alkyl ethers: use 3°-ONa + 1°-X (NOT 1°-ONa + 3°-X $\rightarrow$ elimination).
Anisole (PhOMe) EAS: o/p directing, activating (stronger than -OH? No, -OH is stronger donor).
Glycerol + KHSO$_4$ $\rightarrow$ acrolein (CH$_2$=CH-CHO); sweet smell, test for glycerol.
Lucas works only on ROH soluble in reagent (≤ C$_6$); larger alcohols are insoluble.
traps: Phenol does NOT react with NaHCO$_3$ (not acidic enough); RCOOH does — CO$_2$ evolved distinguishes them.
Ethers are CLEAVED by HI (not HCl/HBr at RT): R-O-R$'$ + HI $\rightarrow$ R-I + R$'$OH (I$^-$ attacks less hindered).
Anisole + HI: gives CH$_3$I + PhOH (NOT PhI + MeOH — aryl C-O is stronger).
Phenol + Br$_2$ (aq) $\rightarrow$ 2,4,6-tribromophenol instantly (white ppt); in CS$_2$ gives mono-Br.
Glycol (1,2-diol) + HIO$_4$ $\rightarrow$ cleaves C-C between OHs (Malaprade); used in carbohydrates.
Peroxide in old ether: tests positive with KI/starch; distil carefully — explosion risk.
examDayCheck: Acidity fastest sort: -NO$_2$/-COOH/-X on ring pushes acidity UP; -OCH$_3$/-CH$_3$ pushes DOWN.
Lucas: 3° = immediate, 2° = wait, 1° = never (at RT).
Williamson: always pair 1°-halide with the hindered alkoxide.
Kolbe = salicylic acid (COOH); Reimer–Tiemann = salicylaldehyde (CHO) — don't swap.

subject: chemistry
summary: Named reactions factory: Cannizzaro, Aldol, Clemmensen, Wolff-Kishner, HVZ, Rosenmund, Stephen.

formulas.name: Rosenmund
formulas.expr: RCOCl + H$_2$ / Pd-BaSO$_4$ (poisoned w/ S/quinoline) $\rightarrow$ RCHO + HCl

formulas.name: Gatterman-Koch
formulas.expr: Benzene + CO + HCl / anhyd. AlCl$_3$/CuCl $\rightarrow$ PhCHO

shortcuts: Tollens' (Ag$^+$/NH$_3$) mirror: aldehydes YES, ketones NO, HCOOH/HCOOR YES.
Fehling's/Benedict's (Cu$^{2+}$, alkaline tartrate): aliphatic CHO YES; aromatic CHO NO; ketones NO.
Iodoform test (I$_2$/NaOH) positive: CH$_3$CO- group OR CH$_3$CH(OH)- group (ethanol, acetone, acetaldehyde YES; methanol, formaldehyde NO).
Nucleophilic addition at C=O: aldehydes > ketones (steric + +I of alkyl).
Acid derivative reactivity toward nucleophiles: RCOCl > (RCO)$_2$O > RCOOR$'$ > RCONH$_2$.
Decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH/CaO (soda-lime), $\Delta$ $\rightarrow$ RH + Na$_2$CO$_3$.
o/p substituents: -NO$_2$ on benzoic acid increases acidity most at p; -OMe decreases at p.
traps: Benzaldehyde fails Fehling's (no aliphatic $\alpha$-H/aromatic) but passes Tollens'.
Formic acid (HCOOH) reduces Tollens', Fehling's AND decolourises KMnO$_4$ — it's an aldehyde-acid hybrid.
Cannizzaro needs NO $\alpha$-H (HCHO, PhCHO, (CH$_3$)$_3$CCHO); aldol needs $\alpha$-H.
Clemmensen fails with -NO$_2$, -OH (acid-sensitive); Wolff-Kishner fails with base-sensitive groups.
Schiff's reagent: aldehydes restore pink; acetone does NOT (but cyclohexanone sometimes does weakly).
Acetic acid freezes at 16.6 °C ('glacial'); melting point is NOT 0 °C.
2,4-DNP (Brady's): gives orange-yellow ppt with ALL aldehydes & ketones — detect carbonyl, not distinguish.
examDayCheck: Tollens' distinguishes CHO from C=O; iodoform distinguishes CH$_3$CO- or CH$_3$CH(OH)-.
Cannizzaro vs Aldol: no $\alpha$-H → Cannizzaro; has $\alpha$-H → Aldol.
Clemmensen = acid; Wolff-Kishner = base. Pick the one your substrate tolerates.
Order reactivity of acid derivatives: Cl > anhydride > ester > amide.

subject: chemistry
summary: Basicity orders, Hinsberg, carbylamine, diazotisation — the small-chapter-big-marks specialist.

formulas.name: Gabriel phthalimide
formulas.expr: Phthalimide-K + R-X $\rightarrow$ N-alkyl phthalimide $\xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+ / \text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2}$ R-NH$_2$ (only 1°, NO aryl)

formulas.name: Hofmann bromamide
formulas.expr: RCONH$_2$ + Br$_2$ + 4 KOH $\rightarrow$ R-NH$_2$ + 2 KBr + K$_2$CO$_3$ + 2 H$_2$O (loses 1 C)

formulas.name: Carbylamine
formulas.expr: R-NH$_2$ + CHCl$_3$ + 3 KOH $\rightarrow$ R-NC + 3 KCl + 3 H$_2$O (1° amines only, foul smell)

formulas.name: Hinsberg (PhSO$_2$Cl)
formulas.expr: 1° $\rightarrow$ sulfonamide soluble in KOH; 2° $\rightarrow$ insoluble sulfonamide; 3° $\rightarrow$ no reaction

formulas.name: Diazotisation
formulas.expr: Ar-NH$_2$ + NaNO$_2$ + 2 HCl $\xrightarrow{0-5\text{°C}}$ ArN$_2^+$Cl$^-$ + NaCl + 2 H$_2$O

shortcuts: Basicity in GAS phase: 3° > 2° > 1° > NH$_3$ (pure +I effect).
Basicity in AQUEOUS phase: (CH$_3$)$_2$NH > CH$_3$NH$_2$ > (CH$_3$)$_3$N > NH$_3$ (+I vs H-bonding vs steric).
Aromatic amines MUCH less basic than aliphatic: lone pair conjugated into ring (resonance).
Aniline basicity: p-toluidine > aniline > p-nitroaniline (EWG destabilises ArNH$_3^+$).
Aniline does NOT undergo Friedel-Crafts (AlCl$_3$ binds N; ring deactivated by ArNH$_3^+$).
traps: 3° amines give NO reaction in Hinsberg test (no N-H); they dissolve in acid — separable by shaking with HCl.
Carbylamine (isocyanide) test detects 1° amines ONLY, not 2° or 3°.
Aryl diazonium is STABLE at 0–5 °C; aliphatic diazonium decomposes instantly → alcohol + N$_2$.
Reduction of -NO$_2$: Sn/HCl or Fe/HCl gives Ar-NH$_2$; Zn/NH$_4$Cl gives hydroxylamine Ar-NHOH; Zn/NaOH gives azo/hydrazo intermediates.
Aniline + Br$_2$ (aq) $\rightarrow$ 2,4,6-tribromoaniline (white ppt) — acetylation (to acetanilide) first enables mono-bromination.
Gabriel gives ONLY 1° aliphatic amines; fails for Ar-NH$_2$ (aryl halide doesn't do SN2).
examDayCheck: Basicity in water: 2° > 1° > 3° (methyl) or 2° > 3° > 1° (ethyl).
Hinsberg: 1° dissolves in KOH, 2° does not, 3° doesn't react.
Below 5 °C — ArN$_2^+$ is your exam-time gateway to -Cl/-Br/-I/-CN/-OH/-H/azo dye.
Hofmann bromamide loses a carbon; Gabriel keeps the carbon count.

subject: chemistry
summary: Sugars, amino acids, proteins, nucleic acids, vitamins — pure memorisation; 100% from NCERT.

formulas.name: Glycosidic bond
formulas.expr: Maltose: α-1,4; Lactose: β-1,4 (gal-glu); Sucrose: α-1,2 (glu-fru); Cellulose: β-1,4; Starch/glycogen: α-1,4 + α-1,6 branches

formulas.name: Peptide bond
formulas.expr: -CONH- formed between $\alpha$-COOH of one AA and $\alpha$-NH$_2$ of next (dehydration)

formulas.name: Amino acid zwitterion
formulas.expr: H$_3$N$^+$-CHR-COO$^-$ (isoelectric point pI: neutral form dominant)

formulas.name: DNA bases
formulas.expr: Purines: A, G; Pyrimidines: C, T (U in RNA); pair: A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds)

shortcuts: Reducing sugars: glucose, fructose, maltose, lactose (free CHO/OH at anomeric C) — positive to Tollens'/Fehling's.
Non-reducing: SUCROSE only (both anomeric OH locked in glycosidic bond).
Fructose is a KETOSE but still reduces Tollens' (tautomerises to aldose in base).
Starch = amylose (linear α-1,4) + amylopectin (branched); glycogen = highly branched animal starch.
Cellulose has β-1,4 — humans lack β-glucosidase, cows/termites have microbes.
Essential AAs (must eat): 'PVT TIM HALL' — Phe, Val, Thr, Trp, Ile, Met, His, Arg*, Leu, Lys (Arg partially).
Secondary structure $\alpha$-helix/β-sheet — stabilised by H-bonds; tertiary by S-S, ionic, H-bonds.
traps: Vitamin B$_{12}$ contains Co (cobalt), NOT Zn or Fe. Haem has Fe; chlorophyll has Mg.
Scurvy = Vit C (water-soluble); Rickets = Vit D (fat-soluble); Beriberi = Vit B$_1$; Pellagra = Vit B$_3$.
Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E, K ('ADEK'). Rest are water-soluble (B complex, C).
Glucose exists as 36% $\alpha$-pyranose, 64% $\beta$-pyranose in solution — NOT open-chain (explains why glucose doesn't give NaHSO$_3$ adduct or Schiff's test).
DNA: 2'-deoxyribose + A/G/C/T; RNA: ribose + A/G/C/U (U replaces T).
Denaturation breaks 2°/3°/4° (H-bonds, disulfide) but NOT 1° (peptide bonds intact).
Enzymes are globular proteins (except ribozymes = RNA); their activity is pH/T sensitive.
examDayCheck: Sucrose = only common non-reducing sugar; hydrolysis = 'invert sugar'.
B$_{12}$ has Co; haemoglobin has Fe; chlorophyll has Mg.
Glycogen = animal storage; starch = plant storage; cellulose = plant structure.
A-T (2 H-bonds), G-C (3 H-bonds) — GC-rich DNA is more stable.

subject: chemistry
summary: Colour, magnetism, oxidation-state trends, lanthanoid contraction, K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ and KMnO$_4$ reactions.

formulas.name: Lanthanoid contraction
formulas.expr: Gradual decrease in atomic/ionic radius from La to Lu (poor 4f shielding)

shortcuts: Colour of Mn: Mn$^{2+}$ pale pink, Mn$^{3+}$ violet, MnO$_2$ black, MnO$_4^{2-}$ green, MnO$_4^-$ purple.
Colour of Cr: Cr$^{2+}$ blue, Cr$^{3+}$ green/violet, CrO$_4^{2-}$ yellow, Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ orange.

Colour of 3d ions (aq): Ti$^{3+}$ purple, V$^{3+}$ green, Cr$^{3+}$ violet, Mn$^{2+}$ pink, Fe$^{2+}$ pale green, Fe$^{3+}$ yellow, Co$^{2+}$ pink, Ni$^{2+}$ green, Cu$^{2+}$ blue, Zn$^{2+}$ colourless.
Highest oxidation state of 3d: Mn = +7, Fe = +6, after Fe it drops. Ru, Os go to +8.
Transition-metal trends: max OS up to Mn, then drops; successive IEs small; most form complexes; most are paramagnetic.
Lanthanoid contraction effect: Zr ≈ Hf radius; 4d and 5d same-group similar size — hard to separate.
traps: KMnO$_4$ is PURPLE because of charge-transfer (LMCT), NOT d–d (Mn is d$^0$ in +7).
Cu$^{2+}$ (d$^9$) has 1 unpaired $\rightarrow$ paramagnetic, BLUE; Cu$^+$ (d$^{10}$) colourless but less stable in water (disproportionates to Cu + Cu$^{2+}$).
Zn, Cd, Hg are NOT typical transition metals (d$^{10}$ in ground state and all common OS — no partial d).
Hg is LIQUID at RT; Ag has highest electrical/thermal conductivity (not Cu!).
Lanthanoids show +3 as stable state (some show +2/+4: Ce$^{4+}$, Eu$^{2+}$, Yb$^{2+}$, Tb$^{4+}$).
Actinoids are more reactive & show wider oxidation states than lanthanoids due to poorer 5f shielding.
K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ is a primary standard (not KMnO$_4$ — it's non-stoichiometric with MnO$_2$ impurity).
examDayCheck: Colour from d–d $\rightarrow$ need partial d. d$^0$ and d$^{10}$ are colourless (except LMCT species like MnO$_4^-$).
Lanthanoid contraction makes 4d ≈ 5d radii — key to Zr/Hf, Nb/Ta similarity.

subject: chemistry
summary: Nernst, Kohlrausch, Faraday; battery chemistry and corrosion. Easy marks if equations are automatic.
shortcuts: Positive E° = reduction favoured (oxidising agent); more positive = stronger oxidiser. F$_2$ strongest (+2.87 V).
For concentration cell: E = (0.0591/n) log(C$_{\text{anode}}$ / C$_{\text{cathode}}$) — runs till concentrations equalise.
1 F deposits 1 mol of monovalent metal (Ag, Na); 2 F for divalent (Cu, Zn); 3 F for Al.
Strong electrolytes: $\Lambda_m$ rises slightly on dilution (Debye-Hückel-Onsager); weak: rises SHARPLY near infinite dilution.
Order of $\lambda^{\infty}$: H$^+$ (349.8) > OH$^-$ (198.6) > others (Grotthuss proton hopping).
Sacrificial protection: Zn/Mg protects Fe (Zn oxidises preferentially — galvanisation).
Lead storage: Pb + PbO$_2$ + H$_2$SO$_4$ discharging; charging reverses it. H$_2$SO$_4$ density drops on discharge.
traps: Salt bridge prevents accumulation of charge and maintains electrical neutrality — it does NOT carry electrons.
In electrolytic cell, cathode is -, anode is +. In galvanic, cathode is +, anode is -. (Cathode = reduction always.)
On aqueous electrolysis of NaCl (brine), CATHODE gives H$_2$ (not Na — H$_2$O has lower reduction potential... actually higher/less negative); ANODE gives Cl$_2$ (overvoltage effect beats O$_2$).
Standard hydrogen electrode: Pt, H$_2$ (1 atm), H$^+$ (1 M), E° = 0 (defined).
$\Delta$G° = -nFE°: if E°_{cell} > 0 (spontaneous) then $\Delta$G° < 0 and K > 1.
Fuel cell efficiency > engine (70% vs 40%); H$_2$-O$_2$ gives water — no pollution.
Corrosion: Fe $\rightarrow$ Fe$^{2+}$ at anode (pit); O$_2$ + H$_2$O + 4e$^-$ $\rightarrow$ 4OH$^-$ at cathode (rim).
examDayCheck: Nernst at 25 °C: coefficient is 0.0591/n — commit to memory.
$\Delta$G° = -nFE°; positive E° $\Rightarrow$ negative $\Delta$G° $\Rightarrow$ spontaneous.
1 F = 96500 C deposits 1 equivalent (Eq = M/n).
Salt bridge = charge neutrality, NOT electron flow.

subject: chemistry
summary: Integrated rate laws, half-life tricks, Arrhenius — pure plug-and-chug once you've memorised four formulae.
shortcuts: Units of k: zero = mol L$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$; first = s$^{-1}$; second = L mol$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$; n-th = L$^{n-1}$ mol$^{1-n}$ s$^{-1}$.
Half-life shortcuts: n = half-lives; amount left = $[A]_0/2^n$ (first-order only — but for any order, after 1 t$_{1/2}$, half remains).
For 10× rise in T (or typical 10 K): rate roughly doubles (rule of thumb, $E_a$ ≈ 50 kJ/mol).
If order is 0 in a species, changing its conc does NOT change rate; doubling species of order n multiplies rate by 2$^n$.
Pseudo first-order: one reactant in huge excess (e.g., water in ester hydrolysis).
Elementary step: order = molecularity. Complex reactions: order $\neq$ molecularity (can be fractional or zero).
traps: Molecularity is for elementary reactions only, always a whole positive integer; order is experimentally determined and can be zero, fractional, or negative.
For a zero-order reaction, rate is independent of conc but NOT independent of time ([A] drops linearly).
t$_{1/2}$ of first-order depends ONLY on k, not on starting concentration.
Activation energy $E_a$ is the SAME for forward and reverse in absolute terms only if $\Delta H = 0$; generally $E_{a,f} - E_{a,r} = \Delta H$.
Catalyst lowers $E_a$ for BOTH forward and reverse equally — doesn't shift equilibrium, just reaches it faster.
Rate constant depends on T (Arrhenius) and catalyst; NOT on concentration.
Graph: ln k vs 1/T is linear with slope $-E_a/R$.
examDayCheck: First-order: t$_{1/2}$ = 0.693/k; use log form for percentage decomposition.
For 'how many half-lives?': remaining = $[A]_0/2^n$ — solve for n.
Arrhenius: higher $E_a$ $\Rightarrow$ more T-sensitive. Doubling T can shoot k up hugely.
Order from units of k: s$^{-1}$ = first; L mol$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$ = second.

subject: chemistry
summary: Raoult, colligative properties, van't Hoff — numeric gold. Four questions are almost guaranteed.

formulas.name: Raoult's law
formulas.expr: p_A = x_A \cdot p_A° ; \; p_{total} = x_A p_A° + x_B p_B°

formulas.name: Henry's law
formulas.expr: p = K_H \cdot x \; (\text{solubility of gas in liquid})

shortcuts: Ideal solution: $\Delta$H$_{mix}$ = 0, $\Delta$V$_{mix}$ = 0, obeys Raoult at all x (e.g., n-hexane + n-heptane).
Positive deviation: weaker A-B interaction, +ve $\Delta$H$_{mix}$, $p_{obs} > p_{Raoult}$ (e.g., ethanol + acetone, CHCl$_3$ + C$_2$H$_5$OH).
Negative deviation: stronger A-B (H-bond), -ve $\Delta$H$_{mix}$, $p_{obs} < p_{Raoult}$ (e.g., CHCl$_3$ + acetone, HNO$_3$ + H$_2$O).
K$_b$ (H$_2$O) = 0.52 K kg/mol; K$_f$ (H$_2$O) = 1.86 K kg/mol — memorise.
Van't Hoff i: NaCl = 2, CaCl$_2$ = 3, K$_4$[Fe(CN)$_6$] = 5, glucose/urea = 1. Incomplete diss: use $\alpha$.
For dimerising solute (e.g., RCOOH in benzene), i < 1.
Osmotic pressure is the only colligative property accurate at low M (measurable for biomolecules).
traps: Molarity changes with T (solution volume changes); molality does NOT (uses mass).
Max boiling azeotrope = -ve deviation (HNO$_3$ 68% + H$_2$O, HCl 20.2% + H$_2$O).
Min boiling azeotrope = +ve deviation (ethanol 95.6% + H$_2$O).
Osmotic pressure $\pi$ uses MOLARITY, not molality (unlike $\Delta T_b$, $\Delta T_f$).
Isotonic = same $\pi$; hypertonic shrinks cell (plasmolysis); hypotonic swells cell.
Henry's K$_H$ INCREASES with T for gases (gas solubility DECREASES with T — warm soda goes flat).
For 2% NaCl (i=2) and 1.8% glucose (i=1) both ≈ isotonic — don't forget i when comparing.
examDayCheck: Freezing-point / boiling-point: always include i × K × m.
$\pi$ = iCRT — uses R in the units that match (0.0821 L atm/K/mol typical).
Raoult: positive deviation → min BP azeotrope; negative → max BP azeotrope.

subject: chemistry
summary: Werner, IUPAC nomenclature, CFT splitting, isomerism, magnetism — algorithmic once you know the rules.
shortcuts: Spectrochemical series (weak to strong): I$^-$ < Br$^-$ < S$^{2-}$ < SCN$^-$ < Cl$^-$ < F$^-$ < OH$^-$ < H$_2$O < NH$_3$ < en < NO$_2^-$ < CN$^-$ < CO.
Strong field ligands (CN$^-$, CO, NO$_2^-$, en, NH$_3$) cause low-spin, pairing; weak field (H$_2$O, F$^-$, Cl$^-$) high-spin.
[Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{4-}$: low-spin, d$^6$, DIAMAGNETIC (0 unpaired); [Fe(H$_2$O)$_6$]$^{2+}$: high-spin, 4 unpaired.
Tetrahedral complexes are ALWAYS high-spin ($\Delta_t < P$); sq planar usually low-spin (d$^8$: Ni$^{2+}$, Pt$^{2+}$, Pd$^{2+}$).
Colours from d-d: Cu(H$_2$O)$_6^{2+}$ blue; + NH$_3$ $\rightarrow$ deep blue Cu(NH$_3$)$_4^{2+}$ (stronger field, shorter wavelength absorbed).
Chelate effect: en ligand gives bigger K than two NH$_3$ (entropy win).
Ambidentate: -NO$_2$ (nitro) vs -ONO (nitrito); -SCN (thiocyanato-S) vs -NCS (thiocyanato-N).
traps: IUPAC: write cation first, anion second; within formula, ligands alphabetically; Greek prefixes don't affect order.
En counts as 2 coordination sites (bidentate), but one ligand in naming (bis for complicated, di for simple).
Geometrical isomerism needs $\geq$ 2 different ligands; [Ma$_6$] or [Mab$_5$] cannot show it.
Optical isomerism in octahedral: common in [M(en)$_3$]$^{n+}$ and cis-[M(en)$_2$X$_2$]; trans usually has plane of symmetry.
[Ni(CN)$_4$]$^{2-}$: d$^8$, sq planar, diamagnetic; [NiCl$_4$]$^{2-}$: d$^8$, tetrahedral, paramagnetic (2 unpaired).
Charge of complex ion: $\sum$(oxid. state of M) + $\sum$(charges of ligands) = overall charge.
Back-bonding: CO is $\sigma$-donor + $\pi$-acceptor; makes M-C bond short and M-O stretch lower.
examDayCheck: IUPAC: alphabetical ligands, oxidation state in Roman, complex cation before anion.
Strong ligand = low-spin; tetrahedral = always high-spin.
Cis-[Ma$_2$b$_2$] sq planar is optically inactive; cis-[M(en)$_2$b$_2$] oct is chiral.

subject: chemistry
summary: VSEPR geometry, hybridisation, MO diagrams, dipole, bond order — NCERT visual memory.

formulas.name: Formal charge
formulas.expr: \text{FC} = V - \dfrac{B}{2} - L \; (V=\text{valence e}^-, B=\text{bond e}^-, L=\text{lone e}^-)

formulas.name: Bond order (Lewis)
formulas.expr: \text{BO} = \dfrac{\text{total bonds in all res. structures}}{\text{number of res. structures}}

formulas.name: Hybridisation shortcut
formulas.note: V=valence e-, M=monovalent atoms, C=cation, A=anion charge

shortcuts: VSEPR geometries: 2=linear (sp), 3=trigonal planar (sp$^2$), 4=tetrahedral (sp$^3$), 5=trigonal bipyramidal (sp$^3$d), 6=octahedral (sp$^3$d$^2$).
With lone pairs: AX$_4$ = tet; AX$_3$E = pyramidal (NH$_3$); AX$_2$E$_2$ = bent (H$_2$O); AX$_5$E = sq pyramidal; AX$_4$E$_2$ = sq planar.
Bond angles compressed by lone pairs: CH$_4$ (109.5°) > NH$_3$ (107°) > H$_2$O (104.5°).
MO: N$_2$ BO=3, paramagnetic? NO (diamagnetic); O$_2$ BO=2, paramagnetic (2 unpaired in $\pi^*$).
MO ordering: up to N$_2$, $\sigma_{2p_z}$ ABOVE $\pi_{2p}$; from O$_2$ onward, $\sigma_{2p_z}$ BELOW $\pi_{2p}$.
Polarity: symmetric molecules with equal bonds $\Rightarrow$ $\mu$ = 0 (CO$_2$, BF$_3$, CH$_4$, SF$_6$).
H-bonding strength: F-H > O-H > N-H; ortho-nitrophenol has intra H-bond (lower BP than para-isomer).
traps: CO$_2$ is linear, $\mu$ = 0; H$_2$O is bent, $\mu$ = 1.84 D. SO$_2$ is bent (lone pair), $\mu$ ≠ 0.
NH$_3$ dipole > NF$_3$ dipole (lone pair aligns WITH N-H bonds but OPPOSES N-F bonds).
Hybridisation changes with geometry, not bonding. In graphite C is sp$^2$; diamond sp$^3$.
BeCl$_2$ in vapour is linear (sp), but in solid is polymeric (sp$^3$, chain).
Ne$_2$ bond order = 0 (N$_b$ = N$_a$), so Ne$_2$ doesn't exist as a bonded molecule.
Fajan's rule: more covalent if cation small/high-charge, anion large/high-charge. AgCl has more covalent character than NaCl.
sp$^3$d uses d orbital for expansion (SF$_4$, PCl$_5$) — only possible from period 3 onwards (d orbitals needed).
examDayCheck: Count lone pairs + bond pairs = hybridisation: 2→sp, 3→sp$^2$, 4→sp$^3$, 5→sp$^3$d, 6→sp$^3$d$^2$.
O$_2$ is paramagnetic in MO theory (2 unpaired); N$_2$ is diamagnetic.
Bond length inversely related to bond order: triple < double < single.
H-bond > dipole-dipole > London dispersion.

subject: chemistry
summary: First and second laws, state functions, Hess's law, spontaneity criterion. Numerical-heavy.

formulas.name: First law
formulas.expr: \Delta U = q + w \; (w = -P_{ext}\Delta V \text{ for P-V work})

formulas.name: Enthalpy
formulas.expr: H = U + PV; \; \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT

formulas.name: Heat capacity
formulas.expr: q = n\,C_p\,\Delta T \; (\text{const P});\; q = n\,C_v\,\Delta T \; (\text{const V})

formulas.name: C$_p$ − C$_v$
formulas.expr: C_p - C_v = R \; (\text{ideal gas, per mole})

formulas.name: Entropy change
formulas.expr: \Delta S = \dfrac{q_{rev}}{T}; \; \Delta S_{universe} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} > 0 \text{ for spontaneous}

shortcuts: State functions: U, H, S, G, T, P, V. Path functions: q, w.
Signs: work ON system is +; heat ABSORBED is +. Expansion does - work on system.
$\Delta$H > 0 endothermic; $\Delta$H < 0 exothermic. $\Delta$S > 0 when disorder rises (gas formation, dissolution of most salts).
Spontaneity by $\Delta$H, $\Delta$S: $\Delta$H<0,$\Delta$S>0 always spontaneous; $\Delta$H>0,$\Delta$S<0 never; mixed cases depend on T.
For ideal gas isothermal: $\Delta$U = 0, $\Delta$H = 0, q = -w.
Hess: $\Delta$H total = $\sum\Delta$H steps, regardless of path.
Bond enthalpy: $\Delta_r H$ = $\sum$(bonds broken) - $\sum$(bonds formed).
traps: Combustion gives $\Delta$H$_c$, always negative; formation of an element in std state = 0 by definition.
$\Delta$S fusion (solid$\rightarrow$liquid) and vapourisation are positive; freezing, condensation negative.
For reversible adiabatic process, $\Delta$S$_{sys}$ = 0 (no heat exchange, q$_{rev}$ = 0).
$\Delta$G° at equilibrium = 0 (at the point where Q = K), but $\Delta$G° refers to standard conditions and is generally NOT zero.
Enthalpy of neutralisation (strong acid + strong base) = -57.1 kJ/mol (const); weak acid gives less (some E used to ionise).
Third law: entropy of perfect crystal at 0 K = 0. Residual entropy exists for imperfect solids (e.g., CO).
$\Delta$H = $\Delta$U only when $\Delta$n$_g$ = 0 (e.g., H$_2$ + Cl$_2$ $\rightarrow$ 2HCl; 2 mol gas both sides).
examDayCheck: Spontaneous: $\Delta$G < 0. Equilibrium: $\Delta$G = 0. Non-spontaneous: $\Delta$G > 0.
Isothermal ideal: $\Delta$U = 0, q = -w = nRT ln(V$_2$/V$_1$).
Adiabatic: q = 0, so $\Delta$U = w.
$\Delta$G° = -RT ln K — use to go between K and standard free energy.

subject: chemistry
summary: K$_p$/K$_c$, Le Chatelier, pH/pOH, buffers, K$_{sp}$ and common-ion — quick numerics.
shortcuts: Le Chatelier: increase P favours side with FEWER moles of gas; increase T favours endothermic direction.
Adding inert gas at const V: no shift (partial pressures unchanged); at const P: shift toward more moles.
Catalyst: reaches equilibrium faster, DOES NOT shift position.
Salt of SA + SB (NaCl): neutral; SA + WB (NH$_4$Cl): acidic; WA + SB (CH$_3$COONa): basic; WA + WB: depends on K$_a$ vs K$_b$.
Common-ion effect: adding common ion SUPPRESSES dissociation/solubility (e.g., CH$_3$COOH + CH$_3$COONa).
Ionic product IP vs K$_{sp}$: IP > K$_{sp}$ $\Rightarrow$ precipitation; IP < K$_{sp}$ $\Rightarrow$ more can dissolve.
Buffer capacity is MAX when pH = pK$_a$ (i.e., [salt] = [acid]).
traps: K depends only on T; not on concentrations or pressures.
For gaseous reactions where $\Delta n_g = 0$, K$_p$ = K$_c$.
pH < 7 does not always mean acidic — only at 25 °C. K$_w$ rises with T, so neutral pH at 60 °C is < 7.
Dilution shifts salt solubility by the common-ion law, but adding a DIFFERENT ion may also shift (salt effect — advanced).
Conjugate base of very strong acid (HCl) is a very WEAK base (Cl$^-$) — essentially neutral.
Buffer range: pK$_a$ $\pm$ 1; outside that, buffer fails.
K$_a$ of H$_2$S: first stage K$_{a1}$ ≈ 10$^{-7}$, second K$_{a2}$ ≈ 10$^{-14}$; use in sulfide precipitation problems.
examDayCheck: Henderson: pH = pK$_a$ + log([salt]/[acid]). At pH = pK$_a$, salt = acid.
K$_p$ = K$_c$(RT)$^{\Delta n}$ — sign of $\Delta n$ matters.
pH + pOH = 14 (25 °C); neutral = 7.

subject: chemistry
summary: Electronic effects, stability orders, IUPAC, reactive intermediates — the skeleton of every organic question.

formulas.name: Hyperconjugation
formulas.expr: \text{No. of } \alpha\text{-H directly donates to C}^+ \text{ or to ring via H-C bond break-free delocalisation}

shortcuts: Acidity of RCOOH: EWG at $\alpha$-C increases acidity (Cl$_3$CCOOH > CCl$_2$HCOOH > CClH$_2$COOH > CH$_3$COOH).
Basicity of amines (aq): 2° > 1° > 3° for Me-amines (steric + solvation trade-off).

EAS directors: ACTIVATING o/p: -OH, -OR, -NH$_2$, -NR$_2$, -R, -Ar. DEACTIVATING o/p: halogens (lone pair donates by R, but -I stronger). DEACTIVATING m: -NO$_2$, -CN, -CHO, -COR, -COOH, -SO$_3$H, -NH$_3^+$, -CF$_3$.
Acidity ordering: RCOOH > H$_2$CO$_3$ > ArOH > H$_2$O > ROH > HC$\equiv$CH > H$_2$ > NH$_3$ > CH$_4$.
IUPAC priority (for principal chain): COOH > COOR > COCl > CONH$_2$ > CN > CHO > C=O > OH > NH$_2$ > C=C > C$\equiv$C > halogen.
Degree of unsaturation: DoU = (2C + 2 + N - H - X)/2; used to guess presence of rings/double bonds.
Aromaticity (Hückel): planar, cyclic, conjugated, (4n+2) $\pi$ electrons (n=0,1,2,...).
traps: Halogens are o/p directors AND ring deactivators — resonance donor but stronger inductive withdrawer.
-NH$_2$ activates ring strongly, but PROTONATED -NH$_3^+$ (in acidic Friedel-Crafts) deactivates strongly and becomes m-director.
Hyperconjugation counts $\alpha$-H (on sp$^3$ C next to positive/unsaturated C), not $\beta$-H.
Tautomerism needs $\alpha$-H (keto-enol); acetone (has $\alpha$-H) tautomerises, but 2,2-dimethylpropanal does not.
Benzyne intermediate: symmetric, so in NaNH$_2$ cleavage of chlorobenzene, nucleophile can attach at either C of triple bond $\rightarrow$ isomeric products.
Most-stable resonance structure: max covalent bonds, min charge separation, negative charge on more-EN atom.
Electromeric effect is TEMPORARY (present only when an attacking reagent is there); mesomeric is PERMANENT.
examDayCheck: Acidity ladder: RCOOH > ArOH > H$_2$O > ROH > HCCH > NH$_3$.
Cation stability: 3° > 2° > 1° (hyperconjugation + +I).
o/p directors = activating EXCEPT halogens (deactivating o/p).
Aromatic: planar, cyclic, continuous $\pi$, (4n+2) electrons.

subject: chemistry
summary: Alkanes-alkenes-alkynes-benzene reagent match; Markovnikov, ozonolysis, Wurtz, Kolbe, Lindlar.

formulas.name: Markovnikov
formulas.expr: CH_3CH=CH_2 + HBr \rightarrow CH_3CHBrCH_3 \; (\text{H to less-subst, X to more-subst})

formulas.name: Friedel-Crafts alkylation
formulas.expr: Ar\text{-H} + R\text{-X} \xrightarrow{AlCl_3} Ar\text{-R} \; (\text{needs activated or benzene; fails on deactivated or aniline})

formulas.name: Friedel-Crafts acylation
formulas.expr: Ar\text{-H} + RCOCl \xrightarrow{AlCl_3} Ar\text{-COR} \; (\text{no rearrangement, stops at mono})

shortcuts: Baeyer's reagent (dilute alkaline KMnO$_4$, cold): decolourised by alkenes/alkynes (forms diol/diketone); alkanes inert.
Br$_2$/CCl$_4$ test: decolourises with C=C and C$\equiv$C; alkanes/aromatics don't.
Terminal alkyne: has acidic C-H ($\alpha$-H on sp C); gives white ppt with AgNO$_3$/NH$_3$ (Ag acetylide) and red with Cu$_2$Cl$_2$/NH$_3$.
Internal alkyne: NO reaction with Tollens'-like tests (no acidic H).
Ozonolysis tells position of C=C: products $\leftrightarrow$ two halves of original alkene.
Benzene EAS rank: HNO$_3$/H$_2$SO$_4$ (nitration); conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ (sulfonation); Cl$_2$/AlCl$_3$ (halog.); RCl/AlCl$_3$ (alkyl.); RCOCl/AlCl$_3$ (acyl.).
Alkanes: highly symmetric, low BP; branching lowers BP; n-C$_n$H$_{2n+2}$.
traps: Markovnikov applies to unsymmetrical additions of HX, H$_2$O, etc.; symmetric reagents (Cl$_2$, Br$_2$) give no regiochemistry issue.
Anti-Markov only with HBr + peroxide. HCl and HI peroxide don't flip (bond-dissociation energies wrong).
Lindlar is for cis (syn addition, poisoned); Na/liq.NH$_3$ gives TRANS alkene (anti-addition).
Ozonolysis of alkyne gives carboxylic acids (oxidative) or aldehydes (reductive with Zn/H$_2$O).
Friedel-Crafts fails on aniline (AlCl$_3$ complexes with N) and strongly deactivated rings (nitrobenzene, benzoic acid).
Carbocation rearrangement in FC alkylation: 1° $\rightarrow$ 2° $\rightarrow$ 3° (via H/alkyl shift) — acylation does NOT.
Benzene ring does NOT decolourise Br$_2$ water (aromatic; stable $\pi$); it substitutes only with Lewis acid.
examDayCheck: Markov = H to H-rich C; Anti-Markov = HBr + peroxide only.
Terminal alkyne: white ppt w/ Tollens'-like (Ag); internal: silent.
Ozonolysis reductive (Zn/H$_2$O) $\Rightarrow$ aldehydes/ketones; oxidative (H$_2$O$_2$) $\Rightarrow$ acids/ketones.
Lindlar = cis; Na/liq.NH$_3$ = trans.

subject: chemistry
summary: Bohr, de Broglie, uncertainty, quantum numbers, Aufbau/Hund/Pauli — plug-and-chug numerics.
shortcuts: Quantum numbers: n (1,2,3..), l (0 to n-1), m$_l$ (-l to +l), m$_s$ ($\pm$1/2).
Subshell capacity: s=2, p=6, d=10, f=14 (from orbitals x 2).
Aufbau: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s.
(n+l) rule: lower (n+l) fills first; if tie, lower n first. Explains 4s before 3d.
Exceptions: Cr [Ar]3d$^5$4s$^1$, Cu [Ar]3d$^{10}$4s$^1$ (half/full d more stable).
Hydrogen spectrum series: Lyman (UV, n$_1$=1), Balmer (visible, n$_1$=2), Paschen (IR, n$_1$=3), Brackett (n$_1$=4), Pfund (n$_1$=5).
H-alpha (Balmer, n=3→2): $\lambda$=656.3 nm (red).
traps: Photoelectric effect: depends on FREQUENCY (not intensity) above threshold $\nu_0$; below $\nu_0$, no electrons regardless of intensity.
de Broglie applicable to all matter but significant only for small m, high v (electrons, not macroscopic).
Bohr model works only for H-like ions (single e$^-$): H, He$^+$, Li$^{2+}$, etc. Multi-electron atoms need screening.
Quantum mechanical orbital SHAPE: s (spherical), p (dumbbell), d (4 lobes or donut), f (complex).
Node count: total nodes = n-1; angular = l; radial = n-l-1.
Isoelectronic species (same electron count): O$^{2-}$, F$^-$, Ne, Na$^+$, Mg$^{2+}$, Al$^{3+}$ all have 10 e$^-$.
Pauli: no two electrons in atom can have all four q.n. same; so max 2 electrons per orbital (opposite spins).
examDayCheck: Balmer is visible; Lyman is UV; Paschen/Brackett/Pfund are IR.
de Broglie: $\lambda = h/mv$ (bigger m or v $\Rightarrow$ smaller $\lambda$).
Orbitals in shell n: $n^2$. Electrons: $2n^2$.
Cr and Cu are the classic exceptions to Aufbau — half-filled/filled d.

subject: mathematics
summary: Standard integral table, definite-integral properties (King's rule), by-parts (ILATE) and special forms — highest-yield Math chapter in KCET.

formulas.name: Trig (memorise block)
formulas.expr: $\int\sec^2 x\,dx=\tan x;\;\int\csc^2 x\,dx=-\cot x;\;\int\sec x\tan x\,dx=\sec x$

formulas.name: By parts (ILATE)
formulas.note: Order: Inverse-trig, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential

formulas.name: Periodic
formulas.expr: $\int_0^{nT} f(x)\,dx = n\int_0^T f(x)\,dx$ if $f$ has period $T$

shortcuts: Standard Result: $\int_0^{\pi/2} \frac{\sin^n x}{\sin^n x + \cos^n x} dx = \frac{\pi}{4}$ (Works for any n, even fractional).
Leibniz Rule: $\frac{d}{dx} \int_{a(x)}^{b(x)} f(t) dt = f(b(x))b'(x) - f(a(x))a'(x)$.
See ∫dx/(a²+x²)^(3/2) → substitute x = a tan θ (denominator becomes a³ sec³ θ).
See ∫dx/(a²−x²)^(3/2) → substitute x = a sin θ.
∫₀^{π/2} sinⁿx/(sinⁿx+cosⁿx) dx = π/4 by King's rule — answer is independent of n.
If integrand is f(sin²x, cos²x)·sec²x, divide N and D by cos²x and sub t = tan x.
For ∫(px+q)/(ax²+bx+c) dx — split as A·d/dx(denom) + B·(const).
∫xⁿe^x dx: Iₙ = xⁿe^x − nIₙ₋₁ (reduction).
Symmetric trig limits: ∫₀^π x·f(sin x) dx = (π/2)∫₀^π f(sin x) dx.
Don't split a log/inverse-trig integrand — apply by-parts with dv = dx (ILATE puts them first).
traps: ∫dx/x = ln|x|+C — absolute value is required; missing bars loses a mark.
∫sec x dx ≠ ln|sec x|; it is ln|sec x + tan x| (confused with ∫tan x).
King's rule needs the limits to be fixed numbers — not valid for indefinite integrals.
In Walli's, when n is odd the factor π/2 is NOT included.
Periodicity integral shortcut fails unless lower limit is a multiple of T (shift first if not).
∫_{-a}^{a} (odd)·(even) dx = 0 because product is odd — don't compute brute-force.
After a substitution, always transform the limits; don't back-substitute then re-plug.
examDayCheck: Scan each integral for symmetry (odd/even) and King's rule before touching the pen.
If there's an e^x factor, look for f(x)+f'(x) structure — collapses to e^x f(x).
ILATE order: if 'ln x' or 'tan⁻¹ x' is present, it is u.
Always add +C on indefinite integrals (KCET graders sometimes include decoy options).
For ∫1/(ax²+bx+c) dx, complete the square FIRST — then match the standard form.

subject: mathematics
summary: Tangent/normal, monotonicity, maxima-minima, approximation — 3–4 direct questions per paper.

formulas.name: Approximation
formulas.expr: $f(x+\Delta x) \approx f(x)+f'(x)\Delta x;\;\; \Delta y \approx dy = f'(x)\,dx$

formulas.name: Sphere / cone / cylinder
formulas.expr: $V_{\text{sph}}=\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3,\;S=4\pi r^2;\;V_{\text{cone}}=\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h;\;V_{\text{cyl}}=\pi r^2 h$

shortcuts: Tangent parallel to x-axis ⇒ dy/dx = 0; parallel to y-axis ⇒ dx/dy = 0 (or m_T = ∞).
For 'shortest distance from point to curve' problems, minimise d² (not d) to avoid square roots.
If f'(x) doesn't change sign at a critical point, it's neither max nor min (inflection).
For closed interval absolute max/min, evaluate at endpoints AND critical points.
Sphere/cube 'relative error' shortcut: ΔV/V = 3·Δr/r (or 3·Δa/a).
Minimum surface-area cylinder of fixed volume: h = 2r (diameter = height).
Volume of box from square sheet of side a, cut squares of side x: V = x(a−2x)²; max at x = a/6.
traps: f'(c)=0 is NECESSARY but not sufficient for extrema — check sign of f'' or sign change.
A function can be increasing even where f'(x) = 0 at a single point (e.g., x³ at 0).
Slope of tangent to x = f(y) is dy/dx = 1/f'(y) — not f'(y).
Angle between curves is measured at their POINT OF INTERSECTION — solve the system first.
MVT needs continuity on [a,b] AND differentiability on (a,b) — strict-vs-closed distinction.
Increasing on an OPEN interval allows f'(x) ≥ 0 (equality at isolated points is fine).
examDayCheck: Rate problem: write the relation, differentiate w.r.t. t, THEN substitute known values.
Maxima/minima word problem: write the target function in one variable before differentiating.
Check if the question asks for slope, tangent equation, or normal equation — don't conflate.
Read 'strictly increasing' vs 'monotonically increasing' — affects equality sign on f'.

subject: mathematics
summary: Standard limits, L'Hôpital, continuity/differentiability piecewise checks — 3–4 Qs each KCET.

formulas.name: Differentiability
formulas.expr: $f'(a^-)=f'(a^+)$ must both exist & be equal (also implies continuous)

formulas.name: Sandwich theorem
formulas.expr: $g\le f\le h,\;\lim g = \lim h = L \Rightarrow \lim f = L$

shortcuts: Expansion Snippets: $\sin x \approx x - x^3/6$, $\cos x \approx 1 - x^2/2$, $e^x \approx 1 + x + x^2/2$.
Standard Limit: $\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{1-\cos mx}{x^2} = \frac{m^2}{2}$.
Any trig-in-trig limit (sin/tan of f(x) → 0): replace sin(f) ≈ f, tan(f) ≈ f.
cos(f) ≈ 1 − f²/2 for f → 0 — use for 1−cos forms.
1^∞ form: compute limit of exponent · (base − 1).
|x|, [x] (greatest integer), {x} (fractional) are prime continuity-check targets — always test both sides.
Rational limit at infinity: divide numerator & denominator by highest power of x.
If f is differentiable, it IS continuous — but not vice-versa. So checking differentiability also settles continuity.
For piecewise f, solve LHL=RHL=f(a) for continuity; then LHD=RHD for differentiability.
traps: L'Hôpital applies ONLY to 0/0 or ∞/∞ — don't apply to 2/0 or 0/∞.
lim sin(1/x) as x → 0 does NOT exist (oscillates).
|x| is continuous at 0 but NOT differentiable at 0 — classic KCET decoy.
Greatest integer [x] is discontinuous at every integer (not just some).
Differentiability does not guarantee f' is continuous (but is rare on KCET).
After using L'Hôpital, if the new form is still 0/0, you may need to reapply — don't stop at first step.
examDayCheck: Identify the indeterminate form first (0/0, ∞−∞, 1^∞, 0·∞) — method follows from form.
For word-form limits, rewrite in terms of basic known limits before brute forcing.
Continuity at endpoints of a piecewise definition — check the matching pieces only.
If a parameter is in the problem (find k making f continuous), set LHL = RHL = f(a).

subject: mathematics
summary: Algebra of matrices, types (symmetric, skew, orthogonal), inverse via adjoint — reliable 2–3 Qs.
shortcuts: Cayley-Hamilton for 2x2: $A^2 - (\text{tr } A)A + |A|I = 0$. Use this to find $A^{-1}$ or high powers of A instantly.
Skew-symmetric matrix of odd order has det = 0 (so non-invertible, always).
For 2×2 inverse: $A^{-1} = \tfrac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{pmatrix}d & -b\\-c & a\end{pmatrix}$ — swap diag, flip sign of off-diag.
Number of symmetric n×n matrices with entries in {0,1,...,k}: (k+1)^(n(n+1)/2).
A + Aᵀ is always symmetric; A − Aᵀ always skew. Use to break into parts.
If A is skew of even order, trace = 0 automatically; det = (det A)².
A² = A and invertible ⇒ A = I.
traps: Matrix multiplication is NOT commutative: AB ≠ BA in general.
(A+B)² ≠ A²+2AB+B² unless AB = BA.
Inverse only exists if |A| ≠ 0 — always check.
(A−¹)ᵀ = (Aᵀ)−¹ — order of operations matters.
A skew-symmetric matrix has all diagonal entries equal to 0 — not just 'some'.
|kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n×n matrix (not just k|A|).
examDayCheck: For 'find k such that A is singular', set det(A) = 0 and solve.
Check order compatibility BEFORE multiplying: (m×n)(n×p) = m×p.
'Idempotent' keywords ⇒ A² = A; 'involutory' ⇒ A² = I.
Read whether matrix is 2×2 or 3×3 carefully — formulas differ.

subject: mathematics
summary: Expansion, row/column operations, properties, solving linear systems (Cramer, matrix method).

formulas.name: Property — swap rows
formulas.expr: $\det$ changes sign when 2 rows (or cols) are swapped

shortcuts: Cyclic Determinant: $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ a & b & c \\ a^2 & b^2 & c^2 \end{vmatrix} = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$. Use to solve algebra-heavy determinants in seconds.
For determinants with 1's in a row/column, expand along that line — kills the arithmetic.
Always try R₂ → R₂ − R₁ or C₂ → C₂ − C₁ first on algebraic dets — often produces zeros.
If a row/column equals (sum of others) × constant, det = 0 instantly.
det(adj A) = |A|^(n−1); det(adj(adj A)) = |A|^((n−1)²).
For 3×3 with cyclic entries (a,b,c in rotations) — factor using a+b+c.
Area of parallelogram with sides u,v = |det[u v]|.
traps: Determinant is a NUMBER, not a matrix — answer can be negative.
|kA| = kⁿ|A|, not k|A|.
If Δ = 0 and one Δₓ ≠ 0, system is INCONSISTENT (not infinite solutions).
If Δ = Δₓ = Δ_y = Δ_z = 0, system may have infinite solutions OR inconsistent — needs rank check.
Row operation R_i → R_i + kR_j keeps det unchanged; R_i → kR_i multiplies det by k.
Area formula has ½ and absolute value — forgetting either is a classic 1-mark loss.
examDayCheck: Expand along the row/column with most zeros or unit entries.
Always write the sign pattern +/−/+ for cofactor expansion.
For 'find k for consistency', set Δ = 0 and solve.
Check: if any two rows/cols identical → det = 0, no computation needed.

subject: mathematics
summary: Conditional prob., Bayes, independence, binomial distribution, mean/variance — 3–4 Qs per paper.
shortcuts: 'At least one' problems → compute complement (no successes) and subtract from 1.
Bayes setup: numerator = prior × likelihood; denominator = sum of all such products.
For 3-coin/5-coin 'exactly k heads' — use binomial C(n,k)(1/2)ⁿ.
Sum of variances for two independent variables: Var(X+Y) = Var(X)+Var(Y).
If P(A|B) = P(A), A and B are independent — useful test.
Two-dice sum = k has P = (# ways)/36; memorise: 7→6/36, 6 or 8→5/36, 5 or 9→4/36.
Expected value of sum = sum of expected values (no independence needed).
traps: Mutually exclusive ≠ independent — usually opposites! Two events that can't both occur are usually dependent.
P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) — Bayes is about swapping these.
In binomial, p + q = 1, but np × nq is NOT npq (variance is npq, not (np)(nq)).
'Without replacement' breaks independence — adjust the second probability.
Odds 3:2 means P = 3/5 (not 3/2) — convert carefully.
For dice problems, the sample space has 36 outcomes (not 11 or 12 despite sum ranging 2–12).
examDayCheck: Read 'exactly' vs 'at least' vs 'at most' carefully.
Check: if the problem gives you P(A|B), Bayes might be required to find P(B|A).
Binomial? Confirm fixed n, fixed p, independent trials, only 2 outcomes per trial.
Variance of binomial: np(1−p) — not np nor n p².

subject: mathematics
summary: Compound/double/half-angle identities, general solutions, sine/cosine rule.

formulas.name: Compound (cos/tan)
formulas.expr: $\cos(A\pm B)=\cos A\cos B\mp\sin A\sin B;\;\tan(A\pm B)=\dfrac{\tan A\pm\tan B}{1\mp\tan A\tan B}$

formulas.name: Double angle
formulas.expr: $\sin 2A = 2\sin A\cos A;\;\cos 2A = \cos^2 A-\sin^2 A = 1-2\sin^2 A = 2\cos^2 A-1$

shortcuts: Memorise specific values: $\sin 15^\circ = \cos 75^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}-1}{2\sqrt{2}}$, $\cos 15^\circ = \sin 75^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}+1}{2\sqrt{2}}$, $\tan 15^\circ = 2-\sqrt{3}$, $\tan 75^\circ = 2+\sqrt{3}$.
a sin x + b cos x = R sin(x+φ), where R = √(a²+b²), tan φ = b/a. Max value = R.
sin(A+B)·sin(A−B) = sin²A − sin²B = cos²B − cos²A.
For 'max of A sin²x + B cos²x' — answer is max(A,B); min is min(A,B).
If sin A = sin B ⇒ A+B = π OR A = B (don't lose one!).
t-method (t = tan(x/2)) turns any rational trig integral into rational in t.
traps: sin(−θ) = −sin θ (odd), cos(−θ) = cos θ (even) — flip sign rule is for sine only.
General solution of sin θ = 0 is θ = nπ (NOT 2nπ).
cos 2A has THREE forms — pick the one with only sin² or only cos² depending on what's asked.
Max of a sin x + b cos x is √(a²+b²), not a+b.
sin²A + cos²B ≠ 1 in general (only when A = B).
In ambiguous triangle case (SSA), two solutions may exist — check both.
examDayCheck: Any 'eliminate θ' problem → use Pythagorean identity after expressing cos and sin.
General solution questions — always include the integer n and the ± / (−1)ⁿ factor as appropriate.
Convert degrees to radians for calculus-related trig Qs (π rad = 180°).
Check the principal value range before writing answer: sin θ = 1/2 principal = π/6, not 5π/6.

subject: mathematics
summary: Principal values, identities, addition formulas — 1–2 Qs but almost always present.
shortcuts: See 2x/(1−x²) → rewrite as tan(2tan⁻¹x). Similarly (1−x²)/(1+x²) → cos(2tan⁻¹x).
Before combining tan⁻¹ values, check if xy < 1 or > 1 — different formula branch.
If sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹y appears, square both sides and use Pythagorean to reduce.
sin(cos⁻¹x) = √(1−x²); tan(sin⁻¹x) = x/√(1−x²) — derive from right triangle mentally.
For inequalities with inverse trig — use monotonicity: sin⁻¹ is ↑, cos⁻¹ is ↓ on their principal ranges.
traps: tan⁻¹(tan x) = x ONLY if x ∈ (−π/2, π/2) — outside, add/subtract π.
sin⁻¹(sin x) = x ONLY if x ∈ [−π/2, π/2] — outside, it's π − x or reflection.
cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x (not −cos⁻¹x like sine).
Sum formula for tan⁻¹ changes by +π or −π depending on signs of x, y — don't ignore.
sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 is ALWAYS true for x ∈ [−1,1] — no restriction needed.
sin⁻¹x domain is [−1, 1], not ℝ — values outside give no real answer.
examDayCheck: Sketch the principal-value branch on a number line before answering.
If the question uses an unusual angle, convert using complementary or negative-argument rule.
Remember sin⁻¹x ∈ [−π/2, π/2] even if the argument came from a larger x (unusual).
For 'Find x: sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹(2x) = π/2' types — apply sin⁻¹A + cos⁻¹A = π/2 trick.

subject: mathematics
summary: Modulus-argument, De Moivre, cube roots of unity, nature of roots, Vieta's.
shortcuts: |z₁+z₂|² + |z₁−z₂|² = 2(|z₁|²+|z₂|²) — parallelogram law.
|z₁·z₂| = |z₁|·|z₂|; arg(z₁z₂) = arg z₁ + arg z₂.
ω² is conjugate of ω; |ω| = 1; (1+ω)(1+ω²) = 1.
i^(4k) = 1, i^(4k+1) = i, i^(4k+2) = −1, i^(4k+3) = −i — just reduce exponent mod 4.
Roots common between two quadratics — use subtract & equate method.
If one root of real-coef quadratic is complex a+bi, other must be a−bi.
traps: arg z must be adjusted for quadrant — tan⁻¹(b/a) alone is not enough (e.g., z = −1 has arg = π, not 0).
De Moivre is valid only for integer n (or rational with care about branches).
Sum of n-th roots of unity = 0 (not 1) for n ≥ 2.
If D ≥ 0 and coefficients real, roots are real — don't write complex form.
α²+β² is (α+β)² − 2αβ — sign of 2 is minus, students write plus.
|z−z₀| = r is a CIRCLE, not a line — classic locus trap.
examDayCheck: For |z−a| = |z−b|, locus is perpendicular bisector of segment ab.
Check if question asks for modulus, argument, or the complex number itself.
When multiplying in polar form, multiply moduli and ADD arguments.
Before solving D<0 quadratic, confirm coefficients are real (else conjugate rule fails).

subject: mathematics
summary: Dot/cross products, projections, angle, coplanarity — 2–3 Qs; overlap with 3D geometry.

formulas.name: Cross product
formulas.expr: $\vec a\times\vec b = \begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\end{vmatrix};\;|\vec a\times\vec b|=|\vec a||\vec b|\sin\theta$

formulas.name: Scalar triple product
formulas.expr: $[\vec a\,\vec b\,\vec c] = \vec a\cdot(\vec b\times\vec c) = \det\begin{pmatrix}a_1&a_2&a_3\\b_1&b_2&b_3\\c_1&c_2&c_3\end{pmatrix}$

shortcuts: Perpendicular check: a·b = 0. Parallel check: a×b = 0.
Direction of a×b by right-hand rule; |a×b| = area of parallelogram on a,b.
Projection SCALAR = (a·b)/|b|; projection VECTOR = [(a·b)/|b|²]·b.
For tetrahedron volume = (1/6)|[AB AC AD]|.
Section formula (internal, ratio m:n): r = (mb + na)/(m+n).
a × (b × c) = (a·c)b − (a·b)c (BAC−CAB rule).
traps: Dot product is commutative; cross product is ANTI-commutative (a×b = −b×a).
|a×b|² + |a·b|² = |a|²|b|² — Pythagoras of vector products.
Scalar triple product sign flips on swapping any two vectors.
a×a = 0 (not 1 or |a|²).
cos θ formula needs magnitudes — forgetting denominator is #1 error.
Unit vector requires dividing EACH component, not just one — always check magnitude = 1.
examDayCheck: Draw a rough mental diagram — especially for 'find angle' or 'find projection'.
For 'coplanar' question, set scalar triple product = 0 and solve.
For 'perpendicular to both' keywords — cross product gives direction.
Angle comes out obtuse? You might need π − θ depending on what 'angle between lines' means.

subject: mathematics
summary: Line & plane equations, angles, distances (point-plane, skew-line SD) — 2–3 Qs.

formulas.name: Angle line ↔ plane
formulas.expr: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\vec b\cdot\vec n}{|\vec b||\vec n|}$ (note: sin, not cos)

shortcuts: Perpendicular from point to plane: foot = point − d·(unit normal).
Plane through 3 points: use det|{x−x₁, y−y₁, z−z₁; …; …}| = 0.
Two planes parallel: normals proportional. Perpendicular: n₁·n₂ = 0.
For coplanar lines (point-line pair a₁, b₁ and a₂, b₂): check (a₂−a₁)·(b₁×b₂) = 0.
Image of point in plane: P' = P − 2·[(P·n−d)/|n|²]·n.
If line is parallel to plane, b·n = 0.
traps: Angle between a LINE and a PLANE uses sin θ (not cos θ) — because angle complements the normal angle.
Direction cosines satisfy l²+m²+n² = 1 — direction ratios DO NOT.
Point-to-plane distance uses |…|; don't drop the absolute value.
Lines being perpendicular means a₁a₂+b₁b₂+c₁c₂ = 0 (direction ratios dot-product).
Two lines may be non-parallel AND non-intersecting → skew. Don't assume intersecting.
If b₁ × b₂ = 0, lines are parallel — use parallel-line SD formula, not skew.
examDayCheck: For angle between line and plane, apply sin θ = (b·n)/(|b||n|) — answer is the complement.
Convert between vector and cartesian forms smoothly — check whether question demands which.
For 'coplanar' with 4 points, use scalar triple product of 3 vectors = 0.
For 'foot of perpendicular' from point to line, parameterise the line and set vector orthogonality.

subject: mathematics
summary: Straight lines, circles, parabola/ellipse/hyperbola — 2–3 Qs; formula-dense.
shortcuts: For tangent to y² = 4ax at point (at², 2at): ty = x + at² — memorise.
Two lines are perpendicular ⇔ m₁m₂ = −1. Parallel ⇔ m₁ = m₂.
Angle between diagonals of ax²+bxy+cy²=0: tan θ = |2√(h²−ab)/(a+b)| where h=b/2.
Circle with diameter endpoints (x₁,y₁), (x₂,y₂): (x−x₁)(x−x₂)+(y−y₁)(y−y₂)=0.
Common chord of two circles S₁ = 0, S₂ = 0 is S₁−S₂ = 0.
For ellipse: sum of focal distances = 2a. For hyperbola: difference = 2a.
traps: For circle x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0: centre is (−g,−f), NOT (g,f).
Radius of circle requires g²+f²−c ≥ 0 — if negative, no real circle.
Ellipse e < 1; parabola e = 1; hyperbola e > 1 — classic comparison.
For horizontal ellipse (a > b), foci on x-axis. For vertical (b > a), foci on y-axis — swap formulas.
Latus rectum of parabola y²=4ax is 4a (length); endpoints (a, ±2a).
Slope formula breaks for vertical lines (x₁=x₂) — handle separately.
examDayCheck: Identify conic type before applying formula — quick sketch helps.
