For 'find circle through 3 points' — plug each into x²+y²+2gx+2fy+c=0 and solve 3×3 system.
Read 'tangent at point' vs 'tangent from external point' — use different forms.
Don't confuse 'directrix' (a line) with 'axis' (another line through focus).

subject: mathematics
summary: Variable-separable, linear, homogeneous — 2–3 Qs; formula-heavy.

formulas.name: Order & degree
formulas.expr: Order = highest derivative; degree = power of highest derivative (after clearing radicals)

formulas.name: General exact
formulas.expr: $M\,dx + N\,dy = 0$ is exact if $\partial M/\partial y = \partial N/\partial x$

shortcuts: If dy/dx + Py = Q doesn't work, flip: dx/dy + P'x = Q' might be linear.
Before integrating-factor, make coefficient of dy/dx equal to 1.
For homogeneous test: replace x → λx, y → λy; if equation unchanged, homogeneous.
Family 'x²+y² = C': differentiate to get xdx+ydy = 0 — use for isocline questions.
Family of concentric circles ⇒ ODE is 2xy/(y²−x²) = dy/dx style (trajectories).
'Growth/decay' problems: dN/dt = kN ⇒ N = N₀e^(kt).
traps: 'Degree' is defined ONLY after the equation is polynomial in derivatives (clear fractional powers first).
Integrating factor e^(∫P dx): forget to include constant — but here we DON'T add +C inside the exponent.
If the DE has y in a transcendental function (e.g., sin y), it's neither linear nor Bernoulli.
'Solution' means general (+ C) unless a boundary condition is given (particular).
Order of (y'')² + y' = x is 2 (not 4); degree is 2.
When separating variables, ensure the variables are fully separated before integrating (no mixed terms left).
examDayCheck: Classify the DE first: separable > homogeneous > linear > Bernoulli > exact.
IF technique: write IF·y = ∫(IF·Q)dx + C — forgetting C loses particular solutions.
For initial-value problem, substitute x₀, y₀ into general solution to find C.
Double-check: order = highest derivative; degree = exponent on that highest derivative term.

subject: mathematics
summary: AP, GP, HP, AM-GM-HM inequality, special series sums.

formulas.name: HP
formulas.expr: Reciprocals are in AP; $T_n$ of HP = $\dfrac{1}{\text{AP term}}$

shortcuts: For 'three numbers in AP': take (a−d), a, (a+d). For GP: (a/r), a, (ar). For HP: reciprocals in AP.
If sum of n consecutive terms of an AP appears, use S_n/n = average = middle term (if n odd).
Telescoping: 1/[n(n+1)] = 1/n − 1/(n+1); sum collapses.
AM ≥ GM equality iff all terms equal — useful for optimisation.
Sum of first n odd naturals = n². Sum of first n even naturals = n(n+1).
Geometric infinite sum only valid for |r| < 1 — check this before applying.
traps: 'Three numbers in GP' — don't take (a−d, a, a+d). That's AP.
G² = AH relates the three means, not A² = GH.
Sum of infinite GP is finite only if |r| < 1 strictly.
In an AP, T_n − T_{n−1} = d (constant difference) — not ratio.
Sum formula for AP uses n/2, not n. And last term is a+(n−1)d, not a+nd.
Sum of cubes = (sum of n)² is special — don't confuse with sum of squares.
examDayCheck: Identify sequence type by checking differences (AP) or ratios (GP) of first few terms.
For 'nth term' questions — use T_n formula; for 'sum', use S_n.
For infinite sum, always confirm |r| < 1.
If problem has AM, GM, HM — use relations between them; don't compute independently.

subject: mathematics
summary: Set operations, equivalence relations, function types (1-1, onto), compositions.

formulas.name: De Morgan
formulas.expr: $(A\cup B)^c = A^c\cap B^c;\;(A\cap B)^c = A^c\cup B^c$

shortcuts: # functions from A to B (|A|=m, |B|=n) = nᵐ. # one-one (if m≤n) = n!/(n−m)!. # onto: inclusion–exclusion.
f(x) strictly monotonic ⇒ injective (and hence invertible on its range).
To test 1-1 algebraically: solve f(x₁)=f(x₂); to test onto: solve y=f(x) for x.
If f has inverse, graph of f⁻¹ is reflection of f across y = x.
Even function f(−x) = f(x); odd f(−x) = −f(x); any f = even + odd parts.
R equivalence ⇒ partitions A into equivalence classes.
traps: (A∩B)^c = A^c ∪ B^c — not A^c ∩ B^c.
{∅} ≠ ∅ — {∅} has one element, ∅ has zero.
A reflexive relation on n elements must have at least n pairs (all (a,a)).
Symmetric but not reflexive relations exist — check carefully.
f: A → B can be onto only if |A| ≥ |B|; 1-1 only if |A| ≤ |B|.
If codomain isn't specified, 'onto' is ambiguous — assume range = codomain.
examDayCheck: For relation problems, list the pairs and check each property individually.
Venn diagram: draw for 2-set and 3-set cardinality Qs.
Composition order: f∘g means g first then f.
For 'find inverse of f(x)', swap x ↔ y then solve for y.

subject: mathematics
summary: Arrangement vs selection, restricted permutations, combinations identities.

formulas.name: Arrangements with repetition
formulas.expr: Words from $n$ letters of which some repeat $p, q, \ldots$: $\dfrac{n!}{p!\,q!\cdots}$

formulas.name: Selection from r kinds
formulas.expr: # ways to pick $r$ from $\infty$ of $n$ kinds: $^{n+r-1}C_r$

shortcuts: Dictionary Rank of a word: Count letters alphabetically smaller to the right, multiply by factorial of remaining positions, divide by factorials of repeating letters.
'At least one' = Total − None.
Word-making 'no two X together' → arrange others first (M slots), then insert Xs into (M+1) gaps: C(M+1, k).
Seating around round table: fix 1 person → (n−1)! linear arrangements of rest.
Choosing and arranging: pick with C, arrange with P or factorial.
Number of rectangles in m×n grid = C(m+1,2)·C(n+1,2). Squares = Σ k·(equiv).
# divisors of N = (a+1)(b+1)... where N = p^a·q^b·...
traps: P = 'order matters'; C = 'order doesn't'. Read carefully — 'committee' (C), 'ranking' (P).
0! = 1 (definition).
With identical items, divide by each repetition factorial — easy to miss one.
Circular: (n−1)! is for distinguishable seats; clasped necklace divides by 2.
'At least' vs 'exactly' — different approaches.
nPr = 0 if r > n; nCr = 0 if r > n.
examDayCheck: Does 'order matter'? If yes → permutation; if no → combination.
Are repetitions allowed? Changes formula drastically.
Is the arrangement linear or circular? Halving for necklaces.
Check restrictive conditions (e.g., 'E always before R') — divide by 2.

subject: mathematics
summary: Expansion, general/middle term, coefficient properties.

formulas.name: Middle term
formulas.expr: $n$ even: one middle = $T_{n/2+1}$; $n$ odd: two middles $T_{(n+1)/2},\,T_{(n+3)/2}$

shortcuts: Term independent of x: set exponent of x in T_{r+1} to 0; solve for r.
Coefficient of x^k in (1+x)^n · (1+x)^m = C(n+m, k) (Vandermonde).
For (a+b)^n, if you want term with 'x^k', substitute actual powers and find r.
Ratio of consecutive binomial coefficients: C(n,r+1)/C(n,r) = (n−r)/(r+1).
If (1+x)^n = ΣaᵣX^r, Σr·aᵣ = n·2^(n−1).
(1+x)^(1/2) ≈ 1 + x/2 − x²/8 + ... for small x (physics approximations).
traps: Middle term: single if n even, TWO middle terms if n odd — students often write only one.
T_{r+1} has ^nCr, power n−r on first term, r on second — keep the indexing straight.
'Coefficient' and 'term' differ — coefficient is the number multiplying the variable.
Term independent of x has x^0, not x^1.
For (1+x)^n binomial expansion is finite if n is a non-negative integer, infinite otherwise.
For (a−b)^n, don't forget the alternating signs: T_{r+1} has (−1)^r factor.
examDayCheck: Write out T_{r+1} with indices explicit before trying to find any specific term.
For 'term independent of x' or 'coefficient of x^k' — set up exponent equation first.
Middle term(s): check if n is even or odd — different number of middle terms.
Substituting x = 1 gives sum of all coefficients; x = −1 gives alternating sum.

subject: mathematics
summary: Area under/between curves using definite integrals — 1–2 Qs, high-yield if practiced.
shortcuts: Always sketch region before setting up integral — identifies which curve is 'top' vs 'bottom'.
For intersection points, equate the curves first.
If region crosses x-axis, split integral — absolute value or sign handled separately.
Symmetric regions: integrate over half and double to reduce computation.
Parabola-chord 'two-thirds rule': area = (2/3) × (base) × (height).
For revolution-like keywords, Pappus's theorem (if ever needed): V = 2π·(distance from centroid to axis)·area.
traps: Area must be non-negative — if ∫f < 0, area is |∫f|.
Identify which curve is 'upper' — swapping gives negative answer.
When integrating wrt y, limits must be y-values (not x).
For region bounded by curve & axis, area = |∫y dx|; for region between two curves, use differences.
Splitting by intersection: if curves intersect more than twice, MULTIPLE subintervals.
Don't forget factor of 2 for symmetric full-region integrals.
examDayCheck: Sketch the region — where curves cross, which is on top.
Set up one integral per subregion; add with correct signs.
Check: does the answer make dimensional sense? (Should be positive.)
For circles/ellipses, use π·a·b shortcut if the region is the full conic.
